t: every living creature, etc.. Specifically an animal without intelligence. But a person is not liable for the damage of his slaves, who have intelligence and he cannot guard them, and if he were liable the slave could damage intentionally and hold his master liable whenever he angers him (Hilchot Genevah 1:9).
when it gores. Pushes or strikes with one of its limbs.
both an ox and any other animal, etc.. The law applies both to an ox and to any animal, beast or bird, although the Torah mentions only an ox (compare below 10:2, 12:1).
only in the usual. In the common and prevalent reality.
like the manner of its creation. As is the nature of animals like it.
amir. The straw (stalk) of the clover plant (Aruch, entry 'amar'; and according to Rashi it seems to be the straw and stubble of grain, see his commentary, Shabbat 76a, Bava Kamma 20a).
in the way of its walking. That it damaged in the course of its regular walking and not in an unusual and deliberate way.

the best of his field... he shall pay. He pays from the best land (and see below 8:10, that one first collects from movables, not necessarily the best, and only if there are no movables does one collect from land).
half damages. For the Torah penalized him to pay part of the damage so that he will guard his animal in the future (Bavli Bava Kamma 15a, and see below 2:7).
from the body of the damager itself. From the value of the damaging animal, after it is sold.
a maneh. One hundred silver dinars.
and the carcass is worth four. So that the total damage is sixteen dinars.
and the carcass is worth a maneh. So that the total damage is one hundred dinars, and half the damage (fifty dinars) is greater than the value of the damaging ox, which is worth only twenty dinars.
the owner of the carcass cannot say, etc.. The injured party cannot demand the entire half-damage payment, since the payment must come from the value of the damaging ox.
rather he says to him. The damager to the injured party.
here is an ox that damaged before you, take it and go. The damager gives him his live ox, and nothing beyond that.
it is called a mu'ad. And the owners must pay full damages from their property.
it is called a tam. And the owners must pay half damages from the body of the animal that caused the damage.
if it became accustomed to the change many times, etc.. Below in chapter 6 it will be explained how an animal becomes a mu'ad for a particular act.
for that matter in which it became accustomed. If it became accustomed to goring it is a mu'ad for goring but not for biting or kicking and the like.
or it became known that it is a goring ox. The verse speaks of an ox that became a mu'ad for goring, and continues by saying that in such a case the damager must pay the injured party full damages.
five complete acts, etc.. Acts in respect of which the animal is considered tam, and only if it becomes accustomed to one of them is it considered a mu'ad for that act.
not to gore, etc.. These damages are among the damages of 'keren' (below halakhah 10).
to push. To push with its body intentionally.
to eat what is fit for it. Kinds of food that it is accustomed to eat (and see below 3:2-3).
to lie on small vessels. Unlike large vessels, on which it is not customary to lie, an animal is a mu'ad to lie on small vessels.
tarbut. That the owner raised in his house.
and trampling. Attacking with the paws of the animal.
and the bardelas. Apparently the reference here is to the hyena (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 1:4, Aruch HaShalem entries 'bardelas' and 'afa').
every mu'ad pays... and every tam pays, etc.. As explained above, halakhah 2.

'and he sends his animal and it grazes in another's field'. The continuation of the verse 'the best of his field and the best of his vineyard he shall pay,' and from the emphasis 'another's' it is learned that if his animal did not damage in another's domain but within his own, he is exempt.
his animal. His beast.
in a courtyard that is not of both of them. But of another person.
or in a courtyard that is of both of them. In which they are partners.
and it is designated, etc.. This courtyard is designated both for placing produce and for bringing animals in.

because it has permission to walk here. It is permitted to walk in the public domain and likewise in the courtyard of both. And even in a courtyard that is not of both, he is exempt because both are equal in this place and the injured party has no more right there than the damager.
if the courtyard of both was designated for produce, etc.. It was agreed that produce may be brought there but not animals.
he is liable even for tooth and foot. For the damager was not permitted to bring his animal there.
and likewise if it was designated for animals for both of them, etc.. That both are permitted to bring animals there but only one is permitted to bring produce.

he is liable even for tooth and foot. For since they agreed on the exclusive right of one to bring in produce, it is as if the courtyard were designated for him and it is like the injured party's courtyard.
three primary categories of damage by an ox. Three groups of damages by animals, each with a 'father' mentioned in the Torah that represents the pattern of the damage.
the horn. Goring, which is the prototype for damages that are not the animal's way to do and involve a change from its usual acts.
and the tooth. That it damaged by eating, which is the prototype for damages from which the animal derives pleasure.
and the foot. Trampling property, which is the prototype for damages done incidentally to its walking.

the derivatives of the horn, etc.. Among the derivatives of the horn is if it ate things not fit for it, such as clothing or vessels, since these acts are a change from the animal's way (see below 3:3).
soiled produce for its pleasure. Relieved itself on the produce (Rabbeinu Chananel, Bava Kamma 3:1). Some explain that it rolled on them for scratching and the like (Rashi there).
damaged with its body in the course of its walking. Its body struck property while it was walking.
with its hair. For example, something stuck in its hair.
with a bridle. A halter.
with the bell on its neck. A bell hanging on it.
and a cart it is pulling. A cart harnessed to the animal and carrying a load, and the cart caused damage.
and in the public domain they are exempt, and in the injured party's domain they pay full damages. As explained above, halakhah 8, the law of foot damages.
like a great shaking that is not its constant way. And therefore it may be that it should be judged as keren.
with its organ. With its genital organ, and while there is indeed no intent to damage, this is a sudden act done in the heat of desire, somewhat similar to keren.

exempt. Because there is doubt here, as explained below, and so we apply the rule that 'the one who seeks to extract from his fellow bears the burden of proof' (see examples below in chapter 9), that if the injured party wishes to extract the money from the damager, the burden of proving his claim falls on him.
and if the injured party seized. That he took the damager's animal on his own, before they came to court.

he collects half damages from what he seized. By the law of keren with a tam animal. And although by strict law the damager is exempt, if the injured party already seized, it is not taken from him. For now he holds the money, and the damager who claims he is right must bring proof to extract it from him.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 8.

both primary categories of damages and derivatives. The law of the primary categories and the law of the derivatives are the same (for details of the primary damages and their derivatives see above 1:10, and below 13:2, 14:1, 14:16).

if the primary category was a mu'ad, etc.. The basic law of the derivatives is that of the primary categories. In damages of tooth and foot, just as the ox is a mu'ad from the start to eat what is fit for it and to break in the course of its walking, so it is a mu'ad for all their derivatives. And in damages of horn, just as the ox is a tam from the start and is not a mu'ad for goring, so it is a tam regarding pushing and biting and the other derivatives of horn.
and all the primary categories of damage and all their derivatives are mu'adim from the start. And they always obligate full damages.
for they are tamim at first until they become mu'adim. Until they become accustomed to this damage and become mu'adim.
as we have explained. Above 1:4-5.

every derivative is like its primary category. Their law is the same regarding the amount of payment (half damages or full damages), the source of payment (from the body of the ox or from the best of the damager's property), and the domains in which one is liable for damage (as detailed above 1:7-9). And see below that the law of derivatives is like that of primary categories also in damages of pit (13:2) and fire (14:16).

except for pebbles that are cast from under the animal's feet. Pieces of earth or other things that are thrown by the animal's walking and cause damage. Although they are thrown as a result of its walking and this damage is similar to foot damages, since the damage is done only indirectly he pays half damages (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 2:1).
and he is exempt for them in the public domain like foot. As explained above 1:8.
he pays from the best of his property. As explained above 1:2.
nevertheless he pays only half damages. And this is the only derivative whose law differs from its primary category, as explained in the next halakhah.
half damages from the best of his property. And not from the body of the ox like the half damages of a tam ox (above 1:2).

and this is a law from the mouth of tradition. It is received in tradition. And this payment is not considered a fine as in keren, but this is the payment due the injured party by the special law of foot (below halakhah 7).
walking in the public domain. And there for foot damages he is indeed exempt.
and pebbles were cast... he pays half damages. Since the pebbles went out into the injured party's domain and damaged there, and in the injured party's domain one is liable for payment.
and it fell on another vessel and broke it. That the pieces of the first vessel fell on another vessel and broke it too.
for the first he pays full damages. Because it was done directly by the animal's trampling, and is judged as foot.
and for the latter half damages. For the pieces of the vessel are considered pebbles, for which one is liable for half damages.
and it kicked and cast pebbles. In this case the pebbles were cast by an unusual act of kicking and not in the course of its regular walking.
and they damaged in the public domain. Where one is exempt for foot damages and liable for horn damages.
exempt. Because of the doubt, as explained below.

and if the injured party seized a quarter damage. That he seized the body of the ox in order to collect from it a quarter of the damage (for horn damages are collected from the body of the ox - Sema, sec. 390:15).
it is not taken from his hand. They leave the money in his hand, even though by strict law the damager would not have to pay (by the law of one who seizes money in a case of doubt, above 1:11).

for the matter is in doubt, perhaps it is a change and not a derivative of foot. There is doubt whether this case is judged as a derivative of foot, in which case he is exempt in the public domain as with foot. Or perhaps, because the damage of the pebbles was done in an unusual way, it should be judged as a derivative of horn, and then he would be liable in the public domain as for horn, and the amount of payment would be a quarter of the damage (for horn damages are paid at half damages, and since this is pebbles one pays half of the usual payment).
and they damaged there. In the injured party's domain, where one is liable both for horn and for foot.

he is obligated to pay a quarter damage, for this is a change in the casting of pebbles, etc.. As stated in the previous halakhah, there is doubt whether this case is considered a derivative of foot or a derivative of horn. And since the damage was done in the injured party's domain, where one is also liable for foot damages, there is doubt whether he is liable for half damages by the law of pebbles from foot, or whether it is defined as a derivative of horn and he is liable for a quarter damage. Therefore, because of the doubt, he pays a quarter damage, but if the injured party seized half the damage it is not taken from his hand.

even if it was walking in a place where it is impossible for it not to cast. For example, on ground full of pebbles, where the animal must cast them. And even though in any case it would have cast pebbles, since it did so in a changed manner, there is doubt whether it is considered a derivative of foot or horn.
whoever pays full damages. For example in all damages of tooth and foot, or in damages of horn when the animal became a mu'ad for them.
the payment is money, as one who borrowed money from his fellow. He has a complete debt, and so the damager must pay the injured party.
and whoever pays half damages. For horn damages when the animal is a tam.
the payment is a fine. And the special laws of a fine apply to it (such as what is explained in the next halakhah, and other laws too - see for example Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8-9).
except for half damages of pebbles. For this payment is not defined as a fine but as money.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 3.
one who pays what he damaged. The value of the damage caused.

and whoever pays more or less. That the amount of payment differs from the amount of the damage (including payments whose amounts are fixed, such as fifty shekels paid by a rapist or seducer - Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:1).
such as double payments. That a thief must pay back twice what he stole.
or half damages. Of a tam ox.
the excess over the principal or the shortfall is a fine. Except for the law of pebbles, which is an exception and is considered money, as explained above.
by the testimony of witnesses. Who will testify that he stole, or that his ox gored, and the like.

but one who admits to any fine from among the fines is exempt. For if he admitted in court before they testified against him, he is exempt (see also Hilchot Genevah 1:5, Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 2:12 and others).
into the air of a glass vessel. Into the hollow of the vessel.
and blew into it and broke it. It let out a loud sound and broke the vessel by the sound waves.
spices. Spices.
pays half damages. For the vessel. If it damaged the food itself, he pays full damages for it, as with tooth damage (and so it appears in several versions of the Rambam here).
for that is its way. Of the rooster, to make a loud noise while eating; and because the damage happened indirectly, he pays half damages, as for pebble-scattering (tzerorot).
this is unusual. For it is not the way of a rooster simply to blow into a vessel.

and pays half damages, as with all fines. This unusual act is treated as horn damage (keren), and he pays the fine of half damages. Although above, halakhah 6, it was explained that for a deviation in scattering pebbles in a private domain one pays a quarter of the damages, this case differs: it is not judged as a deviation in pebble-scattering at all but as horn damage. The reason is that pebble-scattering is indirect damage that occurs incidentally to the animal's normal conduct, whereas here the blowing was done directly, not incidentally to the act of eating, so it is not counted as pebble-scattering. Since it is an act of deviation, it is judged as horn damage and he pays half damages (Yad Peshutah, which thereby resolves the Raavad's objection).
a horse that neighed. That whinnied, made a sound.
and a donkey that brayed. Made the sound of braying.
pays half damages. Under the law of pebble-scattering, since it is the way of animals to make these sounds.
roosters are forewarned to walk in their usual way and to break. Vessels they run into as they walk, and they are liable for full damages under the law of foot damage (regel).
and a vessel became entangled in that thread and was dragged and broke. That as they walked a vessel became entangled in a thread, was dragged along and finally broke.
pays half damages. For this damage is classified as pebble-scattering.
when a person tied it. That the owner of the rooster tied it.
the owner of the roosters is exempt. For it is not his fault and he could not have imagined that the damage would occur.
and if the thread had an owner. And it became tied on its own.

the owner of the thread is liable for half damages, for it is like a pit that rolls. A thread left unattended is considered a pit, since it causes a mishap (see below 13:2), and the owner of the thread who did not put it away is responsible for the damage it caused. Since in this case the damage was done by its becoming tied to the rooster and causing damage indirectly, it falls under the laws of foot damage and is counted as pebble-scattering, for which half damages are due (Arukh HaShulchan 390:15).

and the roosters scratched etc.. Dug in the ground with their feet (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 2:1), and took the thread out of the place where it was hidden, and then it became tangled and tied to their feet.
flying. Flapping about.
if they broke with their wings. That they struck the vessels with their wings.
pays full damages. Under the law of foot damage, since this damage is common and not done intentionally.
and if by the wind of their wings. For example, the wind they created in flight knocked the vessels over and they broke as a result.
pays half damages. Under the law of pebble-scattering, since this is not a direct act but an incidental result of the roosters' flying (as above, halakhah 9).
scratching. Digging with their feet.
and soiled. With their feet.
pecked. With their beaks into the dough or the fruit.
damaged with dirt or pebbles that they raised with their mouths and feet. That as they dug they threw clods of earth from their feet and beaks that caused damage.
they pay half damages. Because of pebble-scattering.
pecking. Fiddling and pecking at a rope to which a bucket is tied.
and the rope snapped. That from so much pecking the rope was cut through entirely.
they pay full damages. Under the law of foot damage.
and it must be that the bucket rolled because of them etc.. That after the roosters pecked at the rope they also pushed the bucket, and it rolled until it broke (Yad Peshutah).
and if there was food on the rope. That edible dirt was stuck to it, and the roosters chewed the rope while eating.

he also pays for the rope. Under tooth damage, since the damage came from a pleasure that is their normal way (but in the first case, he pays only half damages for the rope, since it is done in an unusual way and is treated as horn damage).
full damages. Under the law of foot damage.
forewarned about this matter. To jump from high places downward.
negligence. The owners must guard them well against going up high, because they know they might jump and cause damage, and therefore their going up is classified as negligence.

whatever begins in negligence and ends in accident, he is liable. Although when damage occurs by accident without the owner's fault the owner is exempt, if the act began in negligence it is all judged as negligence and he is liable (for this principle see below 3:11 and elsewhere).
from below upward. They jumped upward and in this way caused damage.
they pay half damages. If they did so in an unusual way, as explained below.
that the kid hung on and clung. Stuck to the wall and caught hold in the cracks and so climbed up, which is not the way of kids.
and the dog jumped. In a single leap, which is what kids do and not dogs.
but if the dog clung and the kid leaped... they are liable for full damages. For this is their way, and he is liable for their damage under the law of foot damage.
and likewise a rooster that leaped... pays full damages. For it is the way of roosters to jump in both these ways.
the flat cake. A thin bread baked on coals, which the dog took with some coals stuck to it.
the stack. A pile of sheaves.
and ate the loaf. The flat cake it took.
and set the stack on fire. That the coals caused the entire stack to burn.
and for the place of the flat cake. The place in the stack where it put the flat cake, which was burned.

pays full damages. For both fall under tooth damage, since the dog's wish to eat caused the loss of the flat cake and its place in the stack (and the Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 23a, says that the flat cake belonged to the owner of the stack and therefore he is liable for it as tooth damage on the injured party's property).

and for the rest of the stack, half damages. Under the law of pebble-scattering (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 2:3), since in placing the flat cake and eating it, the fire from the coal grew stronger and set the whole stack alight, like an animal that scatters pebbles as it walks.
and if it was dragging the loaf over the stack. That while eating it drags the flat cake across the stack.
for the flat cake, full damages. Under the law of tooth damage.
and for the place of the coal. The parts of the stack that were burned by direct contact with the coal.
half damages. Because dragging the flat cake across the stack is an unusual act and he is liable only for half damages, as horn damage.

and for the rest of the stack he is exempt. For unlike the previous case, here the dog dragged the flat cake and did not lift it at all, so that it remained in its owner's domain, and therefore the owner of the dog is not liable for the fire that spread in the rest of the stack (Rabbeinu Chananel, Bava Kamma 22a; for further explanations see Beit Yosef, Mirkevet HaMishneh, Yad Peshutah).
where the owner of the coal guarded his fire etc.. The owner of the coal blocked access to it.
and the dog came and dug. Dug under the door and entered to take the flat cake. In this case the responsibility is on the owner of the dog and not on the owner of the fire.
but if he did not guard his fire. That access to it was exposed.

the owner of the fire is liable for burning the stack. For it was done by the force of the fire that he owns and did not guard properly (for example, where the owner of the fire is not the owner of the flat cake but another person's flat cake was baked on his fire: Rashba, Bava Kamma 23a in the name of the Raavad, and see there for another explanation).
and the owner of the dog is liable etc.. For eating the flat cake and the damage at the place where it was put are tooth damages, for which the owner of the dog is responsible.
one who incites his fellow's dog against another. Who encourages and provokes his fellow's dog to bite another person.
is exempt by human law. The court cannot hold him liable for the damage, since he did not cause the damage with his own force, and the dog is not his that he should be responsible for it.
and liable by the laws of Heaven. Although a court cannot hold him liable, morally he is responsible for what happened and ought to pay.
and the owner of the dog is liable for half damages. As for an innocuous animal (tam) that caused damage by an unusual act.
for since he knows etc.. Since he knew that his dog can be incited against others, he should have guarded it. And since he did not guard it, he is fined half damages.
they provoked. Roused, stirred up.
and if he incited it himself. That the person was bitten because he himself angered his fellow's dog.
for whoever deviates etc.. For the dog deviated and bit because of the deviation of the injured person who incited it himself, and therefore the owner of the dog is exempt.
two cows. Belonging to two different people.
one lying down. That lay down in the middle of the public domain, contrary to the norm.
and the walking one kicked the lying one. While it was walking.

is liable for half damages. The owner of the walking cow is liable under the law of horn damage, and although the lying one deviated by lying down, the owner of the cow that kicked is not exempted by the rule “whoever deviates...” (mentioned in the previous halakhah).

for although it is its way to walk on it, it is not its way to kick it. The exemption arising from the law “whoever deviates” applies only when the first deviation led to some degree to the damage. Indeed, if the animal walked and trampled the lying one, this can be seen as a natural result of the deviation the lying one made. But when the walking one kicked, the kick is unrelated to the lying down of the first, and therefore he must pay half damages.

and it consumes in another's field. The verse speaks of a person's animals that ate and consumed another person's crop. From here we learn that liability applies only on the injured party's property (and compare above 1:7).

and if it benefited etc.. If it ate the fruit in the public domain, although he is exempt from paying for the damage, he must nevertheless pay the injured party what he saved by this eating. For had it not eaten, he would have had to spend money to feed it, as explained below.
and it ate sesame etc.. That it is its way to eat these foods.

lot. In Maimonides' view this apparently means chestnuts or pine nuts (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 7:6, in explanation of the word “lotem”). Some identify it with certain species of the plant called lotem (rockrose) today.
pays a dinar. For that is the full amount of the damage.
and benefited. That the eating was of use to it and did not harm it.

we view them as though etc.. We view it as though it ate basic, cheap food, and he pays the value of such food in the amount his animal ate. For he can say to him that he did not want to spend a lot on food for his animal.

and pays the value of straw or the value of barley. The one who caused the damage may choose the cheaper of the two kinds customarily fed to animals, barley or straw (stalks of clover), and he pays for the amount it ate according to that kind (Maggid Mishneh).

at the cheap price. The price of the kind he pays (straw or barley, as in the version of the Rif, Bava Kamma 8:2 in the pages of the Rif) is fixed at its low rate, which is two thirds of the market price at that time (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 6:23).
ate foods that are bad for it. That its owner would certainly not want to feed it.
exempt. For it caused the damage in the public domain and did not even benefit, and therefore he is completely exempt.
ate foods that are not its way to eat. And eating them is an unusual act with no benefit.

whether on the injured party's property or in the public domain, pays half damages. Under the law of horn damage, for an innocuous animal is liable for half damages for its damage both on the injured party's property and in the public domain.
for this is a deviation. Eating clothing and vessels, and therefore it is treated as horn damage.

and it is the way of people to leave etc.. This explains the reason for liability in the public domain. One might have said that since the first person deviated and left his things in the public domain, the owner of the animal that deviated and ate these things should be exempt (by the principle mentioned above 2:19 that whoever deviates and another comes and deviates against him is exempt). But since it is the way of people to leave their vessels and clothing for a time in the public domain, this is not considered a deviation.

and it plucked fruit from the public domain and ate it on the injured party's property. That the injured party's fruit lay in the public domain, and it brought them into his property and ate them there.

the matter is in doubt. It is doubtful whether we follow the place where it ate the fruit, in which case he is liable for full damages as tooth damage on the injured party's property; or whether we follow the place where the injured party's fruit lay, in which case he is exempt from full damages and liable for what it benefited.
therefore it pays only what it benefited. And he is exempt from the rest because of the doubt, for the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow.
and if he seized etc.. Under the law of one who seizes property in cases of doubt (above 1:11, 2:5-6).
for it ate on his property. And perhaps we follow the place of eating, as stated above.

pays what it benefited. Although the foods lay in a private domain, since it actually ate them in the public domain, he pays what it benefited and not what it damaged. For the laws of tooth damage apply only on the injured party's property.
ate them in the field of the owner of the courtyard. It took the food out of the courtyard to the owner's field, even if far away.
for it ate on the injured party's property. For the injured party's property includes not only his courtyard but all places in his possession.
under pressure. That it does not usually eat them, but in time of hunger it is its way to eat these things too.
vetch. A kind of legume called bitter vetch today.

if it ate on the injured party's property etc.. All the laws of tooth damage apply, for anything that is eaten under pressure, the animal benefits from it and it is considered something that is normally eaten.
and tore. Seized with its teeth in order to eat.
and ate an animal or meat. Whether it ate the whole animal or some of the meat.
for this is its way. To prey on small animals.
this is a deviation. For it is not their way, and since it is unusual, it is treated as horn damage and he pays half damages.
bread. A food that animals eat under pressure.
and a donkey entered. The injured party's courtyard.
and broke the basket and ate the bread. It broke the basket to reach the bread and eat it.
for this is its way. The act of eating requires breaking the basket, and he is liable for everything under tooth damage.
and climbed on the barrel. Climbed on it to reach the turnips.

it is its way to hang on vessels and climb in order to eat. Although above (2:16) it was said that it is not the way of a kid to climb, that was climbing in general; for the sake of eating it is the way of kids to climb (Yad Peshutah).
and afterward broke the basket and ate it. For chewing the basket and breaking it was not part of the process of eating the bread but ordinary damage.
pays full damages for the bread. Under tooth damage.
and half damages for the basket. Under horn damage.
an animal that ate from the open space. That stood in an open space of the public domain and ate.
pays what it benefited. As tooth damage in the public domain.
and even if it turned to the sides of the open space. That it stretched its head to the sides and ate, for this is still considered tooth damage in the public domain.
and went and stood at the sides of the open space. With its whole body there.
pays what it damaged. For this place is considered the injured party's property.
and ate from on top of its fellow. Food that was lying on the back of another animal.
pays what it benefited, for it is the way of animals to eat from on top of one another. And this is like an animal standing in an open space and eating from the sides of the open space.
and if it jumped. That it did not merely bend its head but stood and climbed on its fellow to reach the food.

for the back of its fellow is regarded as the injured party's courtyard. This place is similar to the injured party's courtyard, and when it jumps it enters the injured party's courtyard with its body, and he is liable for full damages, like an animal that left the open space and went to its sides to eat there (Kesef Mishneh).
and fell on fruit and vegetables. Fell on them and thereby damaged them.
or ate. After it fell there.
pays what it benefited. And not what it damaged, since its entering the garden happened by accident and its owner is not at fault.
even if it went from bed to bed etc.. As long as it remained in the same garden he is exempt for its eating, since it entered by accident.
and what benefit does it have from falling. For which it must pay.
for it found a soft place. On top of the fruit and vegetables.
pays what it damaged. For its owner is responsible for its entering there, and this is tooth damage on the injured party's property.
and even if it soiled fruit with the fluids of birth. If it gave birth there and the birth fluids damaged the fruit, though it was forced to do such damage.

because it began in negligence. The animal's entering the garden. And whatever begins in negligence and ends in accident, he is liable (above 2:15). As for liability for acts that are not eating, such as soiling, it has already been explained that tooth damage includes many acts from which it derives pleasure (above 1:10).
and likewise if its fellow pushed it and it fell. That as he was moving his animals from place to place they were crowded together and one was pushed and fell into the garden.
pays what it damaged. Because he was negligent in the way he moved the animals, he is liable even though the fall itself was an accident (Yad Peshutah, and see Hilchot Sechirut 3:9).
slipped and fell. Into the garden.
and left and returned to the garden. And damaged there again.
even though it returned without the owners' knowledge. That he did not see it enter this garden again.

for the matter is known etc.. It is known that if it wanders freely it will go again to the same garden, because it knows the way there and wants to eat there, and therefore its going down there is considered negligence even though it first got there by accident.
the potter who brought his pots into the courtyard of the householder etc.. See below 7:4-7 for similar cases.
and the householder's animal broke them, he is exempt. For a person is not liable for the damage of his animal within his own property (above 1:7).
and if it was hurt by them. The householder's animal.

and if he brought them in with permission he is exempt. For the householder knew that he brought in his pots and should have been careful. However, if the pots were damaged, the householder is not liable for that.
and if the householder accepted upon himself to guard. That he said explicitly that he would watch what the potter brings in.
the householder is liable. Not only is the potter exempt for the damage of the householder's animal, but the householder is also liable for damage to the potter's vessels.
and likewise if he brought in his fruit etc.. The laws of one who brings in fruit mentioned in this paragraph are similar to the laws of one who brings in pots, as explained in the previous halakhah.

he brought them in with permission and the owners of the courtyard left the one they allowed in the courtyard to watch it. That the owner of the courtyard allowed one person to enter with his fruit, and left him alone in the courtyard on the understanding that he would watch what is there.

for since he saw the animal eating harmful things etc.. He should have prevented the animal from eating things that harm it. And since the householder left him there, responsibility for guarding passed to him, and he is liable even though he brought them in with permission.
and they left her and hid so as not to look at her. They went away and left her alone for the sake of modesty, since she uncovers her arms during work.
one who piles a stack in his fellow's field. A field designated for authorized people to put their stacks in, and he made a stack there without permission.
exempt. The owner of the field, since the injured party was not permitted to put his stack there.
it slipped on them and was hurt, the owner of the fruit is liable. If the animal was hurt in a way that is not eating, the owner of the stack is liable for that.
it ate them and was hurt by eating them, he is exempt. As explained above, halakhah 14, the owner of the field's animal had no need to eat from the stack.
the owner of the field is liable. For the damage to the stack.

even though he did not accept upon himself to guard. Unlike what was explained above, halakhah 13, that the householder is not liable for damage until he accepts upon himself to guard, here the law is different.

for the guard of the threshing floors etc.. The guard is the owner of the field himself (Meiri, Bava Kamma 59b; Sma, Choshen Mishpat 393:7), and when he gave permission to put a stack in this place, it is clear that he takes upon himself to guard it, even if he did not say so explicitly, since that is his role there.
with a door that can withstand an ordinary wind. Sturdy enough in an ordinary wind but not in an extreme wind.
and it got out. One of his animals got out in some way.
exempt. For this guarding is generally enough to keep the flock from going out, and since he guarded it properly he is exempt (see below 7:1).
or if the walls of the pen were weak. Even if the door is strong.
he did not lock before them properly. And it was likely that they would get out.
and even if it dug and got out. Dug under the door or under the weak fence.

or robbers broke into it. Bandits. Although these cases are rare and he could not have foreseen them, and so they are classified as accidents, the owner of the flock must pay since he was negligent in guarding them, and a person is liable for what begins in negligence and ends in accident (above 2:15).
a sound partition. Strong, standing in an ordinary wind.
and it was broken through at night... exempt. It is not his fault that the partition was breached in such unusual ways.

the robbers are liable. For once they took it out to steal it, it entered their possession and they are liable to guard it and for its damages in place of the owner. But if they only broke the wall for it and did not actually steal it, they are exempt, since it did not enter their possession (Responsa of Maimonides 432).
if it was a strong and sound fence. And it could not have got out without this breach.

liable. This law differs from the law of the robbers in the previous halakhah, who are exempt if they broke in, because here it speaks of one who broke the fence intentionally so that the animal would go out and cause damage (Responsa of Maimonides 432).
and if it was a weak wall. And liable to fall easily.

exempt by human law and liable by the laws of Heaven. Since the wall was weak, the owners must pay, for it began in negligence. And the one who breached it is liable under the laws of Heaven, since he caused the owners to pay (see there).
and likewise one who gives deadly poison to his fellow's animal. And it ate it and was harmed by it.
exempt by human law etc.. For the animal had no need to eat it (Bavli, Bava Kamma 47b), and he did not perform any act of damage with his own hands, but acted improperly.
one who stations... his fellow's standing grain. Who took his fellow's animal in his hands to another person's standing grain (grain still attached to the ground), and the animal ate from the grain.
the one who stationed it is liable. Although it is not his animal, once he took it to cause damage, he steps into the owner's place to be responsible for it and liable for its damages.
struck it. Hit it with a stick so that it would go to the standing grain.
the one who struck it is liable. For striking is also considered actual leading, and he is the one responsible for its eating the grain.
an unpaid guardian... or a borrower. See their halakhic definition in Hilchot Sechirut 1:1-2.
a paid guardian. A guardian for pay.
they stepped into the place of the owners. To be liable for its damages.
when they did not guard it at all. And because they were negligent, they are liable to pay.
but if they guarded it with excellent guarding, as is proper. Guarding at a higher level than the proper guarding mentioned above, halakhah 1.
the guardians are exempt. For its getting out is classed as an accident, and they are exempt just as the owner is exempt in this case.
they guarded it with lesser guarding. Which is proper guarding, as explained there (see Bavli, Bava Kamma 45a).
if an unpaid guardian... he is exempt. For this is sufficient guarding within the scope of his guarding, since he does not receive pay.

and the owners are liable. It appears that this speaks of an innocuous ox (shor tam) that needs extra guarding to exempt its owner, and ordinary proper guarding is not enough for it (below 7:1), and the owners bear the payment, since they did not hand over to the guardian full responsibility, because his level of guarding is limited (Sma, Choshen Mishpat 396:18).
and even if it killed a person. And its law is to be stoned (below 10:1), and if it is forewarned to kill, its owner also pays ransom (kofer; ibid. halakhah 2).

and if he is a paid guardian, or a renter, or a borrower, they are liable. These have greater responsibility, and therefore if they did not guard the animal with excellent guarding they are liable for the damage (and see Even HaEzel, who explained the whole halakhah differently).
even if it dug and got out and caused damage, he is liable. Although generally he is exempt when it dug in a properly fenced place (above halakhah 1).

for since he left it in the sun etc.. It is known that from the distress of the heat the animal will do everything to escape, and therefore leaving it so is negligence, and the one who left it is liable even if it was well guarded.
delivered his animal to a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor. In order that they guard it. These are considered to lack the understanding to guard.
the owners are liable. For they should not have relied on such people.
for it is the way of an ox and the like to loosen the knot. To pull and play with the rope, and in time the knot may come undone.
even if they guarded it with excellent guarding. By tying and locking.

the owners are liable. For as stated, these guardians lack understanding and their guarding is of no use. The owners should have known that the rope would eventually come undone, and it is their duty to ensure constant supervision of the ox and to watch that it does not get loose. Therefore they are considered negligent in handing over the animal and are liable for all the damage (see Chazon Ish, Choshen Mishpat, Bava Kamma 12:5, Yad Peshutah).
and one of them was negligent. That one of them did not guard properly.
the one who was negligent in guarding it is liable. For his negligence caused the animal to cause damage.
the remaining ones are liable. Since one was negligent in guarding it, each of the others was responsible to guard it.
he borrowed it. A person borrowed an ox from his fellow.
on the presumption that it was innocuous and it turned out to be forewarned. The ox was forewarned (mu'ad) and the borrower did not know it, and the ox gored and caused damage.
if the borrower knew that it is a gorer. He knew it is its way to gore but did not know that it had been formally warned in court and is now classed as a forewarned ox (Torat Chaim, Bava Kamma 40a).

for wherever it goes, its owners' name is on it. Although it passed to the borrower, it is still in the owner's presumption of ownership and remains classed as forewarned (as explained below 6:6). And since the borrower accepted guarding only for the damages of an innocuous ox, the owner is liable for the rest of the damage.
for even if it was innocuous as he thought. Even by his claim, that he thought it was innocuous.
he would have paid half damages, since he knew it is a gorer. And he accepted upon himself responsibility to guard it against these goring incidents.

and if he did not know... the borrower is liable for nothing. For he can say to the owner that he borrowed an ox simply and it did not occur to him that it might gore, and therefore he did not accept responsibility to guard it against goring and to be liable for the damage it would cause (Bavli, Bava Kamma 40a).
and it was forewarned in the borrower's house. That it gored there three times and witnesses testified against it before a court (for the laws of forewarning an ox see below chapter 6).

since its domain changed, the warning is void. Since the warning was done in the borrower's house, it is not valid when it returns to the owner, for the transfer to another domain cancels the warning (below 6:6).
and the owners pay half damages. As for an innocuous ox.
for he returned it. And he has no share in the damage the ox caused.

that he accepted guarding the animal's body only but not guarding its damages. A guardian may stipulate with the owner to limit the responsibility of his guarding (see Hilchot Sechirut 2:9), and he accepted to guard it from being harmed but did not accept to guard it from causing damage to others.
and the owners are liable. For as long as responsibility has not passed to the guardian, the owner is responsible for the damage (as above, halakhah 4).
he accepted guarding its damages. But did not accept to guard it from being harmed.
and the owners litigate with the one who caused the damage. For although the guardian is exempt from the damage, the owner can sue the one who caused the damage himself.
a guardian handed it over to another guardian. To guard in his place, and it went and caused damage.
the first guardian is liable. For he undertook to the owners to stand in their place in guarding the animal from causing damage (above halakhah 4).
for a guardian who hands over to a guardian is liable. See also Hilchot Sechirut 1:4.

and the injured party says to him etc.. The injured party claims his money from the first guardian, who is responsible. However, the guardian may sue the second guardian, who was negligent toward him.
to a member of his household or to his attendant. A person who lives with him or his helper, and it is a person's way to hand over his things to these.
they stepped into the place of the guardian. To be liable for the damages.
for he pays half damages from the animal's body. As stated above 1:2.
the injured party is paid from the animal that caused the damage. The injured party collects the payment from the animal itself, under the usual law for an innocuous ox.
and the value of what the injured party collected remains a debt from the guardian to the owner of the animal. The guardian owes the owner the same amount that the injured party took.
attached fruit. To the ground, which still need to draw from it in order to grow.
we estimate what it damaged in sixtieths. In order to determine the payment for the damage, as will be explained.
we assess sixty beit se'ah in that field, how much it was worth. We estimate: had this land been the size of sixty beit se'ah, what would its value have been with this grain in it (Even HaEzel).
and how much it is worth now, after the se'ah was lost from it. How much that area is worth when it has one se'ah less grain.

and he pays the remainder. The difference. From the verse “and shall consume in another's field” (Exodus 22:4), the Sages learned by tradition that damage done in a field is assessed against another field (Bavli, Bava Kamma 58b). This method is to estimate the damage fairly. For if the se'ah were assessed by itself its value would be much higher, whereas in fact the owner of a large field does not lose so much from this eating; and if it were assessed against a very large area the difference would be too negligible, so they fixed the assessment at sixty, a ratio used for many matters in halakhah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 6:2).
a kav. A sixth of a se'ah.
a quarter. A quarter of a se'ah.
we assess it in sixtieths. For any amount it ate we assess in this way.
fully ripened fruit that no longer need the ground. That finished ripening but are still attached.
pays the value of fully ripened fruit at their worth. As they are worth by themselves, and not in sixtieths, for their law is that of detached fruit.
if it ate the fruit of one palm tree. That had not ripened fully.
and likewise one who cuts down the fruit of his fellow's palm tree and eats it. Although this is a person who robs and damages and not an animal, his law is the same for this matter.

we assess it in sixtieths against the ground. We estimate how much the land is worth with fruit sixty times the amount that was eaten, and how much it is worth without the amount eaten. As is done for fruit that need the ground, as explained above, halakhah 13.

we assess the palm by itself. Because its fruit is fine and expensive, it is not customary to sell it as part of a large piece of land but by itself. Therefore we estimate the value of the fruit by that palm alone and not in sixtieths (Rashi, Bava Kamma 59a).
how much it was worth and how much it is worth now. After its fruit was eaten.
grazing by itself. Alone, not under the supervision of a shepherd.
and entered fields and vineyards. Of others.
they warn its owner three times. To watch his animal against going into others' property.
if he did not guard... the owner of the field has permission to slaughter it. So that it will not damage him.
the Sages forbade raising small livestock and small wild animals. But they permitted raising large livestock (Hilchot Edut 10:4).
in the place of fields and vineyards. Because they spread into the fields and do damage there.
except in forests and deserts in the Land of Israel. These are not settled places, and it is unlikely that people will be harmed there.

and one may raise them in Syria anywhere. Syria is a large region that King David conquered northeast of the Land of Israel, and its law is like the Land of Israel for certain matters but not for this one (see Hilchot Terumot 1:3-4; and see below the law in Babylonia).
ten conditions. That Israelites would treat one another beyond the letter of the law and not insist on their rights.
that one may graze small livestock in forests. That a person may graze small livestock in other people's private forest.
whose trees are large. Forests with large trees, which the animals do not damage much.
but one may not graze large livestock there. For its damage is greater.
except with the knowledge of its owner. That the owner of the forest gives his permission.
that every person may gather wood from his fellow's field. And this is not considered theft.
provided that the wood is poor and close to being thorns. That is of no real use to the owner of the field.
such as hizmei and higei. Kinds of thorns.

provided that they are attached and fresh. Since they draw from the ground, the owner is comfortable with their being uprooted, but for detached ones the owner is particular and wants them (Ramah in Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Kamma 81a).
provided that he does not uproot. That he does not pull up by the roots, since the owner might want them to continue to grow there for some purpose (ibid. in the name of the Geonim).
but other wood is forbidden. For it is valuable to the owner and it is theft (and see Hilchot Melakhim 6:13 for the law in a military camp).

except a field of fenugreek that he sowed for animals. Fenugreek (tiltan) is Greek hay (chilbah), a plant used for human food and animal feed. Since he wants the fenugreek to feed to animals, he wants to feed them with the grasses as well (Bavli, Bava Kamma 81a).
that a person may pinch off a shoot. Cut a branch from a tree to plant it in the ground by him.
except for the olive sprouts. The branches of olive trees that grow at the side of the tree. Since they are easier to root, the owner wants them.

except for the size of an olive and an egg. So reads the manuscript, and it is a difficult text. Some read here “in an olive tree, the size of an egg” (see Yalkut Shinuy Nuschaot in the Frankel edition). Its meaning is that in a large olive tree one may cut branches in such a way as to leave from the branch at its attachment to the trunk a length of an egg (Meiri, Bava Kamma 81a).

from the knot and upward. For in a branch growing from a vine and also in a cane there are knot-like nodes containing buds for renewed growth of the branch, and it is permitted to cut from the knot nearest the branch's emergence and upward (Meiri, Bava Kamma 81a).
from the hidden part of the tree. From the branches at the outer sides of the tree that hide its trunk (Rabbeinu Chananel and Ramah in Shitah Mekubetzet there).
not from its sharp part. The main branch standing in the center of the tree.
from new growth that does not bear fruit. That grew that year and does not yet produce fruit, and therefore there is no loss in cutting it.
and he pinches off only from a place that does not see the face of the sun. He should not take from the outer branches facing the sun, where fruit grows and ripens well (Rashi, Bava Kamma 81b).
for a spring that first emerges. A new spring.

the people of that city in whose boundary it emerged draw from it even though its source is not in their portion. All the people of the city in whose territory the spring is located may use the spring, and not only the owner of the plot in which the spring flows.

and others may not draw from it with them. Residents of another city have no permission to use the spring (and compare Hilchot Gezelah 6:13, that in a spring that flows outside a person's property everyone may use the water that flows out: Yad Peshutah).
from the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Galilee.
he may not spread a net and station a boat there. For fishing is permitted there only in a smaller amount and not by stationing boats and large traps.
except the members of the tribe in whose portion that sea fell. Only the tribe of Naphtali, in whose inheritance the Sea of Galilee fell, may catch in whatever way they wish.
who needs to relieve himself. Who needs to answer the call of nature.
and went behind a fence he came upon. To a private place.
even in a field full of saffron. Which is an expensive spice, and there is great loss if it is damaged.
and takes a pebble from there and wipes. He is permitted to take a clod of earth and wipe himself, and although he might thereby damage the field, he is permitted to do so.
one who strays among vineyards. Who lost his way in his fellow's vineyard.
he cuts and goes up and cuts and goes down. Cuts off the vine shoots to clear a path to get out of the vineyard.

for when mud or puddles increase in the public domain. That from walking on roads in winter, pits full of water form, and even in summer wet mud remains at the edge of the pits, and it is not comfortable to walk like this (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Mikva'ot 9:2; Rashba, Bava Kamma 81b in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel).
to move aside to the sides of the roads. To the edges of a private person's field, even when there are seeds or grain in the field (Rashi there 81a, Tur Choshen Mishpat 274).
a met mitzvah. A dead Israelite who lies abandoned on the road with no one to bury him (Hilchot Evel 3:8), whom everyone is commanded to bury.
acquires his place and is buried in the place where he is found. Even in a private person's field.
the boundary. The border between two fields, and it is not possible to bury him there.
and not within the boundary of the town. Within the limits of the city.
but if he is found on the boundary... he is brought to the cemetery. See Hilchot Tumat Met 8:7 and the rulings and opinions here.
Solomon enacted. Added to the enactments of Joshua.
on paths that have owners. Paths in the fields, by which travelers shorten their way.
until the second rainfall comes. The second rainy season, from which time walking can damage the grain sown in the field.
and these enactments. Of Joshua and Solomon.
and once the dew falls in Babylonia. Where the ground is wetter.
it is forbidden to walk on paths that have owners. Even in the summer as long as dew falls, since trampling is then hard on the ground.
although they do not raise etc.. In fields and vineyards, as said above, halakhah 1.
it is permitted to keep it thirty days before the festival. For he needs meat in honor of the festival.
and before his son's feast. His son's wedding celebration. These occasions justify keeping the animal at home.
and the butcher. A slaughterer who sells meat.
buys and keeps until he slaughters little by little. He buys and keeps the quantity he needs to sell, and so does not keep animals for too long.
provided that it does not go out and graze with the flock etc.. For even this permission is on condition that the animals stay inside the house.
and they have already made Babylonia like the Land of Israel. The Sages of Babylonia ruled that its law is like the Land of Israel.
and not the dog. For it may bite or frighten people. And if he raised a vicious dog he is excommunicated until he gets rid of it (Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14).
in a city near the border. A Jewish city near the border of the country, which needs extra guarding.
by day he ties it and at night he lets it loose. For the main danger is at night, and then there are also no people outside to be concerned about.

cursed is one who raises dogs and pigs, because their damage is great and common. As for pigs, additional reasons were given, such as the incident brought in the Talmud involving a pig sent to the Temple instead of the daily offering (see Bavli, Bava Kamma 82b). In general, the Sages regarded the pig as an extremely loathsome animal.
a shepherd who repented. And animals that he raised in violation of the prohibition remained in his hands.
we do not obligate him to sell immediately. All the animals, because this would cause great loss and he would be deterred from repentance.
gradually. Little by little.
who is considered forewarned. How an animal that has become accustomed to cause damage in a certain way is defined as forewarned, and makes its owner liable for full damages (above 1:4).
whoever has been testified about three days. That it gored on three different days and each day witnesses testified before its owner that his ox gores and he must guard it.
but if it gored on one day or bit etc.. In all of these the ox is innocuous from the start (above 1:5).
even a hundred times. On the same day.
it is not forewarned. For perhaps all the goring resulted from some incidental cause specifically on that day (Meiri, Bava Kamma 23b).
three groups of witnesses testified about it on one day. And each group testified about a goring that took place on a different day (Raavad, Maggid Mishneh).

this is in doubt etc.. It is doubtful whether the requirement of three days is to define the ox as a gorer, and here the gorings really were on three separate days; or whether they are required to warn the owners again to guard the ox, in which case the owner is not liable when all the testimony was given on one day (and see below, halakhah 10, for the law in cases of doubt).
only in the presence of the owners and in the presence of the court. That they testify before him in court that his ox gored.
in court. And specifically a court of ordained judges in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:12).
the ox of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor. Who are not considered of sound mind.
overseas. Abroad.
exempt. For in all these cases the ox is considered to have no owner who would take care to guard it.

guardians. Apotropoi, who will now be responsible for the acts of the ox. [Note: The vocalization of the word follows the Greek original. In the Commentary on the Mishnah in Maimonides' own handwriting there are several vocalizations of this word: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe is not vocalized).]
and they testify about them before the guardians. To inform them that this ox tends to gore and from now on they must be careful and guard it.

they caused damage after they were testified about. After the testimony before the guardian, the ox came under his responsibility, and from now on the count of three times until the ox becomes forewarned begins as usual.

pays full damages from the best of the guardians' property. This speaks specifically of the ox of a minor orphan that caused damage, and since one collects from orphans' property only for special purposes (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 12:1-3), one collects only from the guardian; but if the ox of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or one who went overseas gored, one collects from his property (Yad Peshutah).

and when the orphans grow up they litigate with the guardians and they pay them. Although during their minority they refrain from collecting from their property, they were not thereby released from responsibility for the damage, and therefore the obligation to pay stands.
oxen that are played with etc.. That hold bull fights and train and goad the ox to kill.
are not forewarned for this. The ox does not become forewarned by these gorings, because this killing is done against its will and it is therefore coerced (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 4:3).
and even if they killed a person. For people also take part in these contests and sometimes they are killed.
they are not liable to death. Unlike other killing animals, whose law is stoning (below 10:1-2).
not that they should goad it. Only if the ox killed willingly is it stoned, and not if it was forced to do so (see also there, halakhah 8).
it returned to its innocuousness. And payment for its damages is half damages.
for the change of domain changes its law. And it must be testified about anew in its new domain.
but if he lent it... it stays in its status. As above 4:8, that even if the ox is in the hands of the borrower, the owner's name is still on it.
and the deaf-mute regained hearing. And now he can hear.
and the imbecile became sane. Became rational.
even though the guardian was removed. And the ox returned to their domain.
for it is in its owners' domain. And this is not considered a change of domain, since the guardian is appointed for their benefit and is as their domain.
and it retracted from the matter it was testified about. That it stopped causing damage in this way.

and it returned not to gore... it is innocuous as to goring. For just as an ox can become forewarned for one thing only (above 1:5), so it can return to innocuousness for one matter and remain forewarned for another.
until the children etc.. If children touch it and it does not react angrily and does not cause damage as it used to, it has returned to being innocuous for that damage.
an ox that is forewarned for its own kind. That gored oxen like itself three times.
is not forewarned for what is not its kind. For example, to gore horses and donkeys, for which it is still innocuous.
forewarned for a person etc.. And all the more so, if it was forewarned for an animal it is not forewarned for a person, since it is rarer for an ox to gore people.
forewarned for small ones. Such as calves.
is not forewarned for large ones. Although they are the same kind.
therefore if it damaged a kind for which it is forewarned etc.. And it does not become forewarned for a particular group until it damages it three times.
was forewarned for Sabbaths. That it gored specifically on Sabbath, for example because people look strange in their Sabbath clothes (Jerusalem Talmud, Bava Kamma 4:2).
is not forewarned for weekdays. In fact this law is true for any fixed day on which the ox gores, not only the Sabbath (see Mirkevet HaMishneh and Even HaEzel below, halakhah 10).
and from when is its return. To being innocuous even on the day for which it is forewarned.

it becomes forewarned for everything. For although by three gorings of the same kind the ox does not become forewarned for other kinds, if each day it gored a different kind, it is forewarned for all.
saw an ox today and gored it etc.. It gored three times alternately over six days.
it became forewarned alternately for oxen. And if it gores on two consecutive days, the owner pays for the second day only half damages, as for an innocuous ox (Rashi, Bava Kamma 37a).
saw an ox today and gored it... and on the sixth saw a wild ass and did not gore it. In total it saw six different animals over six days, and of these it gored only three, alternately.
wild ass. A wild donkey.
it became forewarned alternately for everything. Specifically for these three kinds, as explained below.

and if it gored on a day it is forewarned for one of the three kinds it gored alternately. This case is complex: on the one hand, it may be that the ox is forewarned to gore all animals alternately; on the other hand, it may be that it is forewarned for all days but only for the three kinds it gored (and its not goring on the days in between is because it is not its way to gore the animals it saw then). Since this is a doubtful case, the ruling is that the ox is forewarned only for the animals it gored, and that too only alternately (Mirkevet HaMishneh, Even HaEzel).
gored on the fifteenth of this month etc.. That it did not gore on a fixed date but there was a fixed pattern of adding a month and a day between the gorings.

is not forewarned until it triples at skipping. Until it also gores in the fourth month on the eighteenth. For the nature of the gorings is not that they occur on a fixed day but that they occur at fixed intervals (“skips”). Therefore there must be three intervals, which are in practice four gorings (for a similar example see Hilchot Issurei Biah 8:6).
heard the sound of a shofar and gored etc.. That each of the three gorings occurred in response to the sound of a shofar.
it became forewarned for shofars. And there is no concern that it will gore without the sound of a shofar. And if it gored again in this manner, he is liable for full damages.
and likewise anything similar. That it can be forewarned for a particular hour of the day (see Tosefta, Bava Kamma 4:4).
gored three oxen on three days. And became forewarned for oxen.
and on the fourth gored a donkey and on the fifth gored a camel. So that the third goring of the ox can be combined with the gorings of the donkey and the camel.

or it gored a donkey and a camel at first... and afterward gored three oxen. That one can treat the gorings of the donkey, the camel and the first ox as one unit, or alternatively see the three gorings of oxen as another unit.
this is in doubt whether it is forewarned for oxen only. And for other animals he is liable only for half damages.
and on Sunday and on Monday. Immediately after the last Sabbath on which it gored.
or it gored on Thursday on the Sabbath etc.. Here the three Sabbaths come after it gored on weekdays.
this is in doubt whether it is forewarned for Sabbaths only. And not for weekdays, as above, halakhah 8.

or for the three days, two of which are weekdays. Sabbath-Sunday-Monday, or Thursday-Friday-Sabbath, and it follows that it is forewarned not specifically for Sabbaths but for all days (Arukh HaShulchan 389:24).

and all these doubts... we obligate the one who caused the damage only for half damages. Because the ox may still be innocuous, one does not extract from the one who caused the damage more than half damages, by the rule that the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow.
and if the injured party seized... we do not extract from his hand. As stated above 1:11.
with a rope. A cord.
and locked before it properly. See above 4:1 for how this guarding is done.

and if it caused damage in something for which it was forewarned from the start... exempt from paying. For guarding the ox exempts the owner not only from horn damages when the ox is forewarned for them, but also from tooth and foot damages. And not only from these but also from other monetary damages (except for innocuous ox) he is exempt when he guarded properly (Bavli, Bava Kamma 55b; and see above 4:1, below 12:4). As for the reason that for the damages of an innocuous ox he is liable even if he guarded it properly, some wrote that by strict law there is no obligation to guard an innocuous ox at all, since it is presumed guarded, but the Torah fined its owner and obligated him to pay, and so he is not exempt from the fine even when he guarded properly (Minchat Shlomo, Bava Kamma 15:1; and see Meiri, Bava Kamma 45b, who distinguished differently between innocuous and forewarned).
was forewarned for the right horn. That it gored with it three times and became forewarned in this horn.

and gored, whether with the right horn... pays half damages. Since it is innocuous as to the left horn, the status of innocuous still applies to it and extra-careful guarding is required for it. Therefore the duty to guard applies to the right horn as well, and he is liable for its damage as for an innocuous ox, paying half damages from its body (Maggid Mishneh, Even HaEzel, Arukh HaShulchan 396:4).
whether intentionally or unintentionally. See below 11:6.
if it is innocuous etc.. For the law of an ox that injured a person is the same as the law of an ox that injured an ox.
loss of time. What the injured party lost by being unable to work during his illness.
shame. The value of the embarrassment he suffered.
pain. The pain of the blow.
healing. The cost of the cure.
for these four things etc.. These payments are given in addition to the payment for the damage itself, and they apply only where a person injured a person (Hilchot Chovel 1:1).
damages only. The value of what his worth was reduced as a result of the injury.
as will be explained. Hilchot Chovel 1:1, and see there, halakhah 10, that liability for shame applies only to one who intended to embarrass.
and his ox that injured his father or his mother. Of its owner.
is liable for its damages. The value of the injury or of the stack.
whereas if he himself had done this. The person himself.

he would have been exempt from paying. For these acts carry the death penalty for the person who does them, and one who commits a transgression carrying both death and payments is exempt from paying (even if he did the transgression unintentionally and did not actually become liable to death).
as will be explained. Hilchot Genevah 3:1, Hilchot Chovel 4:7.
one who brings his ox into the householder's courtyard etc.. See above 3:13-15 for similar cases.
exempt. The householder, for he had no right to bring his ox there (and see above 1:7).
and if it gored. The ox that was brought in.

as the law of one who gores in the public domain. For horn damages are the same on the injured party's property and in the public domain: an innocuous ox pays half damages, and a forewarned one pays full damages.
fell into the pit... and fouled its water. For example, it was dirty, or it mixed mire and mud into it.

if it fouled it immediately... he is liable for the damage to the water. Full damages under the law of foot damage (Taz 398:4). Some explained that he is liable as horn damage, and the law differs between an innocuous and a forewarned ox (Sma there, 398:3).
and if after a time. That the ox stayed in the water and only then it became fouled, or for example it died and the carcass made the water stink.
the ox became a hazard like a pit. And its law is that of a derivative of pit, for pit damages include obstacles left lying around that cause damage (below 13:2-3).
and we have not found a pit for which one is liable for vessels. From the verse it is learned that one is not liable for a pit that damaged vessels.
as will be explained. Below 13:1-4.
and if he brought it in with permission. His ox, and it damaged the water.
the owner of the ox is exempt. For the owner of the courtyard should have guarded his pit.
and if the householder accepted upon himself to guard. The ox.
he is liable for the damage to the ox. Not only is the ox exempt for the water, but if it was hurt, the owner of the courtyard is liable for that.
or the householder was hurt by it. That he ran into the ox and was hurt by himself.
or it dug. The ox, in its walking, or it opened covered pits.
cisterns, ditches and caves. Different kinds of pits.
the owner of the ox is liable for damages to the courtyard. And likewise for damage to the owner of the courtyard, if it caused him damage.
and the owner of the courtyard is liable for the damage of the pit. If people are hurt by the pit afterward, provided that he had made his property ownerless beforehand (see below 12:2).
for he was obliged to cover it. For it is his property and in his domain, and it is as though he dug it (see below 12:3).
without knowledge. Without awareness or intent.
exempt. Similar to above, halakhah 4, that the fault lies with the one who entered.
and if he damaged it knowingly he is liable for full damages. For a person who damages his fellow's property pays full damages (Hilchot Chovel UMazik 6:1).
because he has the right to remove it etc.. And see also Hilchot Chovel 1:16.
and the dead animal shall be his. From here, the ox that died remains with the injured party, and the one who caused the damage pays him the loss in value.

the decrease in value of the carcass is on the injured party. Since the dead ox belongs to the injured party, if the value of the carcass dropped from the time of death until they stood in court, the injured party bears the loss.

and the increase in value of the carcass is divided by the one who caused the damage and the injured party. Although the carcass belongs to the injured party, when it increased in value, the one who caused the damage and the injured party share the increase.
we assess for damages. We estimate the value of the damage in order to hold the one who caused the damage liable.
whether he or his animal. There is no difference in this between the person who caused damage and his property that caused damage (see Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:15).

rather we estimate how much the vessel lost of its value etc.. The broken vessel remains with the injured party, and we estimate how much it lost of its worth, and the one who caused the damage gives the injured party the whole amount of the loss in the case of a forewarned ox, or half of it in the case of an innocuous ox.
and the carcass was worth at the time of death a hundred. So that the value of the damage is a hundred dinars.
the one who caused the damage pays him only a hundred. According to the damage at the time of death, although the final loss is a hundred and twenty dinars.
and if it was innocuous it pays him fifty from its body. Half of what it lost when it died, and he pays from the body of the ox that caused the damage, as in the law of an innocuous ox's damage.
and it is worth at the time of standing in court a hundred and twenty. So it rose in value by twenty dinars from the time of death.

the one who caused the damage pays him ninety. For the twenty dinars it gained are divided between them, and the one who caused the damage receives ten of them, and he is left to pay ninety out of the hundred he owed.

and this is what is stated... the increase of the carcass they shall divide. They learned from the verse that this does not mean literally dividing the dead ox, but that if it increased in value the one who caused the damage and the injured party divide the increase (see Mishnah Bava Kamma 3:9 and Commentary on the Mishnah there).
and at the time of standing in court it increased in value. It increased in value between the time of the damage and the time of standing in court.
and were it not for this wound. The injury.
it would have been worth eight hundred. For it could have increased in value much more.
that he fattened it. That the injured party spent his own money and fattened the ox.
he gives him only as of the time of the damage. Therefore he will pay twenty-five dinars if it is innocuous and fifty if forewarned.
it grew thin from the blow. That because of the damage of the blow, the ox's value dropped by the time of standing in court.
and the loss is worth a hundred. And not only fifty.

he gives him as of the time of standing in court. For the drop in the ox's value is a result and direct continuation of the blow, and therefore the one who caused the damage must bear the loss and pay according to the time of standing in court.

the one who caused the damage increased in value. The ox that caused the damage. This speaks of an innocuous ox that pays from its body, for example where the ox was not worth enough to cover half the damage and it increased in value until at the time of standing in court it was worth the value of half the damage.

he is paid from it only what it was worth at the time it caused damage. The injured party can collect only from the original value of the ox that caused the damage, and not from what it gained through fattening.

and if it increased in value on its own, half the damage is paid from it as of the time of standing in court. And the injured party can collect half the damage from the full price of the ox as it is worth now.
the one who caused the damage must take trouble with the carcass. As explained below.
he brings up the carcass from the pit. The effort and expenses of bringing up the ox are the responsibility of the one who caused the damage.
and afterward we assess for him the loss in value of the carcass. The difference between the value of the live ox and the value of the carcass.

as it is stated, “he shall pay money to its owner, and the dead animal shall be his”, etc.. They interpreted the verse as though it should be divided: “he shall pay money to its owner and the dead animal” - that the one who caused the damage is obliged to return the loss (“money”) and also the dead ox (“and the dead animal”; Bavli, Bava Kamma 11b).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 9.
an ox belonging to the Temple. That was consecrated to the Temple, as explained below.
his fellow's ox. And it is interpreted as “his fellow's ox” - and not an ox belonging to the Temple (Mishnah Bava Kamma 4:3).

and all sacred things for which one is liable for me'ilah (misuse of sacred property) are not subject to the law of damages. The law of me'ilah applies to things consecrated to the Temple (kodshei bedek habayit) and to things consecrated for offerings (kodshei mizbe'ach): whoever benefits from them commits me'ilah and is liable to pay the principal plus a fifth and to bring a guilt-offering (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:1-3). But among kodshei mizbe'ach there is a distinction between most-holy offerings (kodshei kodashim, such as the burnt-offering or sin-offering), for which there is me'ilah immediately upon consecration, and lesser-holy offerings (kodashim kalim, such as peace-offerings and thanksgiving-offerings), for which there is me'ilah only after the blood is thrown, and even then there is no me'ilah in their meat but only in their emurim (the portions burned on the altar; ibid. 2:1-2). Therefore the law of damages applies to lesser-holy offerings (see the next halakhah).

and disqualified consecrated animals. Sacred animals that were disqualified from being offered on the altar, whose law is to be redeemed and go out to ordinary status (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:10).
for they have gone out to redemption and to being ordinary. And now there is no me'ilah in them (and see below 12:21).
peace-offerings that caused damage. An innocuous ox that is a peace-offering. Peace-offerings are lesser-holy offerings in whose emurim there is me'ilah but not in their meat.
he collects from their meat. Half the damage.
and he does not collect from the meat in proportion to the emurim. As explained in the next halakhah.
for there is me'ilah in the emurim of lesser-holy offerings. If so, the portion of the emurim of the animal that caused damage is exempt, and half the damage may not be collected from it.
as we have explained in Hilchot Me'ilah. 2:1.
and likewise a thanksgiving-offering that caused damage. A thanksgiving-offering too is a lesser-holy offering, and there is no me'ilah in its meat.
