and he does not collect from the bread that comes with it. Together with the thanksgiving-offering one brings forty loaves (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:17-18), and the injured party does not collect from the loaves of the thanksgiving-offering.
for the bread is not part of the meat. The bread does not belong at all to the animal that caused damage, and therefore one does not collect from it.
and how does he collect. How does the injured party take the half damages.

the injured party and his group eat from the meat in holiness in proportion to his half damages. He eats the portion due to him for the damage, for a thanksgiving-offering may be eaten by anyone in holiness.
for if he had to collect in half his damage the worth of a dinar. For example, if the whole damage was worth two dinars.
and all the meat with the emurim was worth two dinars. So it turns out that the payment he collects is half of the body of the entire ox.
and the meat without the emurim was worth a dinar and a half. And if the payment were collected only from the meat portion of half the ox, the sum would be three quarters of a dinar.
he does not collect two thirds of the meat. Which is equal in value to the half damage (a dinar).

but only half of the meat. Since the damage payment required here equals half the value of the ox, half of the ox's body is pledged for payment. But since in this half there are also emurim, from which it is impossible to collect, he actually collects only from the meat portion of the half pledged for payment (Meiri, Bava Kamma 13a).
his fellow's ox. This implies that the ox belongs to a specific person.
and before the injured party seizes it in court. For being ownerless, the injured party could have taken it without a claim, and so it is fitting for him after it damaged his ox.
he is exempt. The person who seized it.
and after it caused damage, he consecrated it. And an ox of the Temple is exempt from damages, as explained above, halakhah 1.
because the gentiles do not hold a person liable for his animal that caused damage. For under their laws a person is not liable for his ox that caused damage.

and we judge them by their own laws. And see Hilchot Melakhim (10:12): when there is a case between an Israelite and a gentile and under one of the legal systems (ours or theirs) the Israelite comes out innocent, we judge according to it.

the injured party collects from it. Since for an innocuous ox the damage is collected from its body, the ox is considered as if its owner had designated it for payment of the damage, and therefore the injured party can collect from it (Bavli, Bava Kamma 33b).

and the buyer goes back and collects from the one who caused the damage who sold it to him. The buyer sues the one who caused the damage to pay him back the price of the ox that the injured party collected from him.

for since it gored, there is a rumor about it, and he should not have bought until the injured party collected. Since it is public knowledge that the ox gored, the buyer should have been careful and concerned that the damage payment would be collected from the ox (and for this reason the injured party can collect from him, although generally when a person designated his ox for his creditor and then sold it, the creditor does not collect from it - see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 18:5).

it is consecrated, so that they will not say that sacred property goes out without redemption. The consecration takes effect, but since the consecration was made on an ox that was previously pledged to the injured party, the consecration does not take effect fully, and the injured party's lien is not entirely cancelled. In any case, the injured party cannot collect from it from the Temple property without redemption, out of concern that people will say that sacred property goes out without redemption, and therefore a symbolic redemption is needed, even for one dinar (commentators, based on Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 7:14-16).
the injured party collects from its meat. Collects the damage payment from the meat.
what is done is done etc.. His law is like one who sells his ox that caused damage, as above, halakhah 6.

it caused damage and stood in court and afterward he sold it, it is not sold etc.. For after standing in court, the injured party has a share in ownership of the ox, and therefore the one who caused the damage cannot transfer the ox to another's domain.
the creditors of the one who caused the damage came first and seized it. For example, the one who caused the damage borrowed money from a person and the lender came first and seized the ox.
whether he became indebted before he caused damage or did not become indebted until he caused damage. It makes no difference whether the loan came before the damage or not.

for even if it was originally the creditors' etc.. For the ox that caused the damage is always pledged to the injured party, in whatever domain it is. In every case in which a person is damaged by the ox, he takes precedence over all other creditors (see Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Kamma 34a in the name of a student of Rabbeinu Perets).

whether it stood in court or did not stand in court... what is done is done. Since the injured party collects the damage from the property of the one who caused it and not necessarily from the body of the ox, he has no share in ownership of the ox, and it is entirely in the domain of the one who caused the damage.
the creditors came first and led it away. As payment of the debt.
for the injured party is paid only from the best of the property of the one who caused the damage. And not necessarily from the ox that caused the damage.

and all his property is pledged for this damage. If so, the ox is only one item among all the other property of the one who caused the damage, which is pledged for payment of the damage, and in this situation the creditors can precede the injured party and seize the ox, for so is the law with movable property (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 20:2).
bran. Grain waste after grinding.
and they collect for the injured party from the poorest land. Inferior land, and orphans have a special law, as explained in the next halakhah.

and movable property is not pledged to a creditor. The rule is that the movable property of the borrower is not pledged for the debt, and therefore one who collects from the heir does not collect from his movable property (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:7).
and if the injured party seized etc.. See there, halakhah 8.
the Geonim already enacted to collect for a creditor from movable property. Even when collecting from heirs (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:11).
they collect for them from the poorest land. From inferior land, and not from the best land, as the one who caused the damage ordinarily pays.
as will be explained. Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 19:1.
and they are not liable for ransom. The owner of a forewarned ox that killed a person is liable for ransom (below 10:2).
and the animal is not put to death. An ox that killed a person is stoned, whether innocuous or forewarned (below 10:1).
so that you not say etc.. That in places where animal damage is common, it is usually people disqualified from giving testimony who are present, and perhaps one would rely on their testimony.
in horse stables. Stables of horses.
slaves and shepherds. Both are disqualified from testimony (see Hilchot Edut 9:4, 10:4).
minors or women. These too are disqualified from testifying (ibid. 9:7, 9:2).
even though this one was gored and this one is forewarned to gore. That the ox found near the dead person is forewarned, and it is reasonable that it gored.
this one was bitten. That the slain ox was found bitten.
and this one is forewarned to bite. And presumably it killed it.
we do not say etc.. Rather, clear proof through witnesses is required.

a camel that is in heat among the camels. It appears that this means a camel in heat, and when in heat the male camels become very wild and fight one another by biting and kicking, so that sometimes they kill each other.
a pregnant animal that caused damage. And it is innocuous, and the owner is obliged to pay half damages from its body.

he collects half damages from it and from its offspring. For the value of the offspring is also taken into account, and if the cow's value is not enough for half the damage, it is collected from the value of the offspring.
because it is from its body. And it is considered part of it, and part of the damaging cause (see Meiri, Bava Kamma 47a and below 11:11-12).
he does not collect from its egg. That was inside it when it caused damage.
because the egg... is separate and set apart. For it is by nature distinct from the body of the bird.
and its offspring was found beside it. After the goring.
if before it gored it had given birth. And the offspring had no connection with the goring.
or after it gored it gave birth. And the offspring was part of it when it gored.
and he does not collect anything from the offspring. For because of the doubt the defendant has the upper hand.

for the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow. One who wants to extract money from his fellow is the one who must bring proof of his claim, and then he will collect from the offspring too.
and its fetus was found fallen beside it. That its fetus died.
or it miscarried because of the goring. And then the fetus is included in the payment for the damage, as explained in the next halakhah.
we do not assess the loss of the cow separately. The difference between its value before the damage and after it.

and the loss of the offspring separately. The gap between a living and a dead offspring. In this way the calculation of the loss is greater since each is assessed separately (Rashi, Bava Kamma 47a). Moreover, even without the goring it is not certain that the fetus would have come out alive (Rabbeinu Baruch the Spaniard there).

rather we assess etc.. We estimate the difference between the value of the cow when it was pregnant and the value of the cow and the dead fetus now. For the goring struck the cow while it was pregnant, and the fetus is to be seen as part of its body (Bavli, Bava Kamma 47a).

the cow belonged to one and the offspring to another. The cow belongs to one person and the offspring to another. And in the loss in value of the cow because it miscarried, a share due to the owner of the offspring is also included, as will be explained.
the loss of fat etc.. The fat that the cow lost from its body because of the goring and the miscarriage.
belongs to the owner of the cow. Because the portion of fat in it is not connected to the offspring itself (Meiri, Bava Kamma 47a).
and the loss of bulk. What the animal lost of its outer bulk, which has economic significance since a larger, fuller cow is paid for at a higher price.
they divide it. Since the offspring too contributed to the animal's large bulk.

and the miscarried fetus belongs to the owner of the offspring. For besides taking into account the fat and bulk of the cow, the value of a pregnant animal is greater mainly because of the offspring it is going to give birth to, and this value belongs entirely to the owner of the offspring. Therefore the owner of the offspring receives the miscarried fetus (as above 7:8) and the one who caused the damage makes up for him the rest of his loss (Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 399:6-7).
perhaps it was hurt by a rock. It may be that the ox was hurt by a rock or the like.

and even though the injured party says etc.. Even if the defendant does not contradict the words of the injured party, the injured party cannot extract money from him until he brings clear proof of his claim.
you surely know that your ox caused the damage. And you are lying and claiming that you know nothing.

he swears a heset oath that he does not know. A light oath (without taking a sacred object) enacted by the Sages of the Talmud, intended for a case where the defendant denies the plaintiff's words and the latter cannot make him swear a severe oath (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:3).

if it was forewarned. For the purpose of the oath is to cause the defendant to admit if he is lying. And indeed for a forewarned ox, the law of one who admits is that he pays, and so the oath will be effective.
but if it was innocuous... he is exempt. Since half damages is a fine and one who admits to a fine is exempt (above 2:7-8), there is no benefit in obligating him by oath.
both are exempt. For the injured party has no one to claim from, since each pushes him off onto the other.
and if both belonged to one man. And it is clear that one of his oxen caused the damage.

from the body of the lesser of the two. In the case that they are innocuous. And since the injured party has no proof which ox gored, the one who caused the damage pays from the body of the lesser one, and if it is not worth half the damage the injured party loses.
and if they were forewarned. Then the value of the ox that caused the damage is not significant for the amount of payment.
where the two oxen are standing. Alive before us.

bring proof that this one standing is the one that caused damage and I will pay you. For it may be that the innocuous one caused the damage and it died or was lost, and if so the one who caused the damage is exempt from paying, for an innocuous ox pays only from its body (and where both are innocuous, it is simple that the one who caused the damage is always exempt until it is known which ox caused the damage).
one large and one small. And both are innocuous.
the large one caused the damage. And half the damage will be paid from its body.
the small one caused the damage. The defendant admits that his ox gored, but according to his claim it was the small ox, and he is willing to pay from the value of its body and no more.
the forewarned one caused the damage. And the required payment is for full damages.

the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow. And in both cases the one who caused the damage is entirely exempt from payment, even though he admitted that one of his oxen caused damage. For since the injured party claims that the other ox is the one that gored, it is as though he says that the first ox, which the one who caused the damage admitted to, did not gore (see below, halakhah 11).
but witnesses testify that one of these two caused damage. And they do not know whether it was the large or small, the innocuous or the forewarned.

the one who caused the damage pays as he said. He pays for the damage of the ox he admitted to. This case differs from the previous halakhah, because here there are witnesses that one of the oxen certainly gored (Maggid Mishneh).

and if the injured party claimed, you surely know that this one caused damage in your presence. That the injured party claimed that the one who caused the damage himself saw that the goring was done by the ox the injured party claims.

the one who caused the damage swears a Torah oath... for he admitted in part. The one who caused the damage must swear by Torah law to be exempt from the rest of the payment. For anyone who denies part of the plaintiff's claim and admits part of it must take a Torah oath (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:1).
the injured parties were two. Innocuous.
the large one damaged the large one and the small one the small one. If so it is reasonable that the damaging oxen will have enough for half the damage.
the small one damaged the large one. And the amount payable for half the damage will not exceed the value of the body of the small ox.
the forewarned one damaged the large one etc.. So that payment for full damages will be greater and half damages smaller. And the one who caused the damage claims the opposite.

the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow. And if there is no proof, the one who caused the damage is entirely exempt even though he admitted that his oxen caused damage, as explained below.

there was no clear proof, the one who caused the damage is exempt. There were no witnesses who identified exactly who gored whom, but they saw that the two gored the two oxen. In this case, though there are witnesses, the one who caused the damage is entirely exempt (Even HaEzel and Yad Peshutah; see their words on the reason for the distinction between this halakhah and above, halakhah 10). Some explain that this halakhah speaks of a case with no witnesses at all, but if there are witnesses that the two gored, though they did not identify exactly who gored whom, the one who caused the damage must pay as he claimed, as above, halakhah 10 (Maggid Mishneh).

to what is this comparable... and is exempt even from the price of the barley, as will be explained in Hilchot To'en. This is the basis of these halakhot: one who claims wheat from his fellow, and the latter denies it but admits that he owes barley, is exempt even from the price of the barley, for by not claiming barley the plaintiff is as though saying that the defendant does not owe him barley (Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 3:10). In any case, the Sages obligated the defendant to swear on the wheat a light oath without taking a sacred object (a heset oath), like any person who denies his fellow's claim (ibid. 1:3).

and if the injured party seized, he is paid... as the one who caused the damage admitted. According to the law explained there. The reason is that by going and seizing, the injured party showed that he was previously imprecise and now retracts his claim and agrees with the one who caused the damage that his claim is correct (Rabbeinu Chananel, Bava Kamma 35b; Yad Peshutah).
for the small from the large. And the same applies to the small from the forewarned in the other case, but Maimonides gave an example.
an ox. Innocuous.

and again gored another ox. Before the one who caused the damage and the injured party managed to divide the price of the ox (and see Even HaEzel and Yad Peshutah on the question whether this speaks of before or after the final judgment).
the first injured party and the owners are like partners in it. And they share responsibility for future damages.
again gored another ox worth two hundred etc.. And the present injured party may also collect a hundred from the price of the ox.
the last one takes a hundred. The amount of half the damage.
and the injured party before him with the owners. Who are counted as partners in the damage.

take fifty each. For since each of them had a share in half the price of the ox (a hundred each), each pays half of the debt to the injured party. That is, each gives fifty to the second injured party, and each is left with fifty dinars.
the last takes a hundred. Half the amount of the damage, as for an innocuous ox.
and the injured party before him fifty. The previous injured party had a share in half the price of the ox (a hundred) and takes part in half the payment - fifty dinars.

and the first injured party with the owners take twenty-five etc.. For each of them had a quarter share of the price of the ox (fifty), and therefore each gives half of his share, and each is left with twenty-five dinars.
and so they divide and go on in this way. One always sees the earlier injured parties as partners with the owners in part of the ox, and each of them pays half of the part he had in the ox.
an injured party who seized the animal that caused damage. Who did not wait for the sale of the ox but took it into his own domain.

became a paid guardian over it for its damages. A paid guardian is responsible for damages the animal causes (above 4:4), and since the injured party brought the animal into his domain, he alone became responsible for its damages.
and it gored again and caused a loss of a hundred and forty. So half the damage due to the last injured party is seventy dinars.
he is paid seventy. He receives seventy dinars as payment for his damage, all from the share of the first injured party.
he is paid the remainder of his damage, which is thirty. Of the hundred dinars due to him, he paid seventy to the second injured party, and so he is left with thirty from his share.
and the owners a hundred. Half the damage done to the first. For the owners are not responsible for what the animal did after it was seized.
and likewise anything similar. Each time the injured party seizes it, all payment for future damage will be collected from his share alone.
two innocuous oxen that injured one another pay the difference as half damages. We estimate how much half the damage of each of them is, and the one whose damage is greater receives the difference.
a forewarned one against an innocuous one. If the full damage owed by the forewarned one is greater than the half damage owed by the innocuous one.
and an innocuous one against a forewarned one. If the half damage owed by the innocuous one is greater than the whole damage owed by the forewarned one.
an innocuous ox that caused a loss to another innocuous ox worth a hundred. And its liability is fifty dinars.
and this last one then caused a loss worth forty. And it is therefore liable for twenty dinars, so the difference between them is thirty dinars.
both were forewarned... sixty. We deduct all the damage done by the second (forty) from all that the first did (a hundred), and he pays sixty.
the first was forewarned. And its full damage is a hundred.
and the last innocuous. And its half damage is twenty.
the first innocuous. And its half damage is fifty.
and the last forewarned. And its full damage is forty.
anywhere. Even in the domain of the one who caused the damage himself (see below, halakhah 11).
exempt according to their laws. For under their law an ox that kills a person is not liable to death, and in this we rule according to their laws (see above 8:5).
both the ox and any other animal etc.. The law of stoning applies to any animal that killed a person. Although the Torah speaks of an ox, the verse speaks only of the usual case (above 1:1).
and the forewarned one is liable for ransom. That the owner is obliged to pay money to atone for his life, as learned from the verse below, halakhah 4.
and since every animal, beast, and bird that killed a person is stoned. Even if innocuous.

how can one be found forewarned to kill etc.. For an ox does not become forewarned until after three times (above 6:1), so how does it come to be forewarned so that a situation arises that obligates its owner for ransom.

for example, it killed three gentiles. And it was not stoned for this, as said above, halakhah 1. But since we saw that it is accustomed to killing, testimony can be given against it and it can be defined as forewarned.

a treifah. A person who suffered a bodily defect from illness or injury and is destined to die from this condition. One who kills a treifah is exempt from death (Hilchot Rotzeach 2:8), and so too an ox that killed a treifah is exempt from death. Nevertheless, since it killed three times, it becomes forewarned.
and afterward it killed a healthy one. A healthy person.
or it killed and fled etc.. It fled three times, and for that reason was not stoned until now.

for the owners are not liable for ransom until the ox is stoned. Therefore if it was not caught the fourth time either, the owners would not pay ransom even though it gored after becoming forewarned. All this applies where the ox is liable to stoning, in which case the owners do not pay ransom until it is actually stoned. But if the ox is not liable to stoning, for example if it killed unintentionally, the owners are liable for ransom when the ox is forewarned even though it was not stoned (below, halakhah 9, Kesef Mishneh here).

and likewise if it endangered three people. It gored three people and did not kill them (and for that reason the ox was not stoned) but brought them to a life-threatening condition. In such a case they are strict regarding ransom, that the ox is called forewarned to kill. For ransom is meant to atone and also arises from the owners' negligence, and one is strict about it (Yad Peshutah in the name of Ralbag, Exodus 21).
as one. On the same day (but not all at once), for in this too they were strict regarding ransom, that the ox becomes forewarned even in one day (Ralbag).
or it killed three animals. And the ox is not stoned for this killing.

this is forewarned to kill. Although above (6:8) it implies that for monetary liability an ox does not become forewarned for people after damaging an animal, the law of ransom is more severe, and the ox becomes forewarned to kill in such a case (Kesef Mishneh).
the witnesses recognized the owner of the ox. They knew that the goring ox was one of this person's oxen.
and did not recognize the ox the first, second, and third time. They did not identify exactly which ox it was, but they knew that the same ox performed the three gorings (Ralbag there, Even HaEzel).
and the fourth time they saw his ox that killed etc.. They again knew that it was one of his oxen, but they were no longer sure whether it was the same one.

since the owners were warned etc.. Since the owner knew that one of his oxen is forewarned to kill, he should have guarded all of them well. Therefore he pays ransom for the last goring, even if the goring ox was innocuous.
this which is stated in the Torah. Regarding a forewarned ox that killed a person.
from tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
by the hands of Heaven. That he is not put to death by a court, and his judgment is left to Heaven.
the ransom of the slain. Ransom according to the worth of the person killed, see below 11:1.
he is atoned for. By the ransom, his sin that his ox caused damage is atoned and he is spared from death at the hands of Heaven.
and although ransom is atonement. Generally, the court is not required to press one who needs atonement to pay (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:17).

we seize the property of one who became liable for ransom against his will. The court intervenes and takes a pledge from the property of the one who caused the damage until he pays. Since the ransom money does not go to the Temple but to his fellow, and moreover here it was not he who sinned but his property, there is concern that the need for atonement will not seem important to him and he will not strive to pay (Bavli, Bava Kamma 40a).

for each of them needs complete atonement. For the ransom does not come for the injured party but for the atonement of the one who caused the damage, and in order to atone for his soul each one brings the full ransom.
we do not finalize the judgment of an ox. We do not rule its sentence to stoning.
the ox of the wilderness. That belongs to no one.
and the ox of the Temple. Belonging to the Temple.

and the ox of a convert who died and has no heirs. A convert has no connection to his former family, and if he did not father children while an Israelite, he has no heir and his property is ownerless (Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 1:6).
and the ox of orphans. Of minor orphans, who are not subject to the laws of damages since they lack understanding, and it is as though the ox has no owner (Or Sameach).
the guardians. Apotropoi, those appointed over the property of others (such as a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor).
and the guardians do not pay the ransom. Even though the ox is stoned.
and minors... are not subject to liability. For all of these are not obligated to guard the ox and are not negligent in its acts.
an ox that is a treifah. Destined to die because of injury or illness (see Hilchot Shechitah chapters 5-10 for the definition of treifah in animals).
or the ox belonged to a person who was a treifah. That the owners are about to die.

as the death of the owners, so the death of the ox. Although the verse was interpreted as dealing with liability to death at the hands of Heaven (above, halakhah 4), it is nevertheless learned from it that the ox's death depends on the law of its owner's liability to death. Therefore where the owner is a treifah and not liable to death (as explained shortly), the ox too does not die. And likewise if the ox itself is a treifah it does not die, just as its owner would not have been liable to death in such a state.

and since its owners are considered as dead and do not need death etc.. For the law is that a treifah person who killed is not liable to death (see Hilchot Rotzeach 2:9). Therefore in the cases mentioned here the ox too is not liable to death, for its law is like its owner's.
one who incites his dog against his fellow. Who encourages and provokes his dog to bite another person.

the dog is not stoned. For liability to death applies only to an animal that kills of its own will and not when it is aroused to do so, in which case it is considered coerced (above 6:5, Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 4:3).
and even if he made it bite him. He opened the snake's mouth and pressed its teeth to his fellow's body.
and killed him. By the venom it released into his body.
for the poison of the snake. The venom.

it spits out on its own. For the venom causes the death and not the bite, and the venom is within the snake's body and it expels it on its own, and although it did so with the person's encouragement and provocation, it did the main killing itself (Arukh HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 405:9).

is exempt from the death penalty of a court. And so too in the case of one who incites, for in all these there is no direct act of killing by the person. But nevertheless “he is a murderer, and the One who seeks blood will seek blood from him” (Hilchot Rotzeach 3:10).
until it intends to harm one for whom it is liable to stoning. And then it is liable even if it intended to kill one person and killed another (Maggid Mishneh).
to kill the animal. For the ox is not stoned for killing it.
and killed the person. By mistake.
intended a gentile. And the ox is not stoned for him (above, halakhah 1).
intended nefalim. An infant born before nine months of pregnancy and not yet thirty days old, one who kills whom is not liable to death (Hilchot Rotzeach 2:6).
or a fine if it killed a slave. An ox that killed a slave or maidservant pays a fixed sum of thirty sela (below 11:1).
since it is forewarned for this. For liability for ransom does not depend on the ox being liable to death but on its having been forewarned and killing, and its owner should have guarded it.
forewarned to fall on people into pits. That it became accustomed to do so.
and saw greens in a pit. The fourth time.
and fell into the pit for the greens. And not in order to reach the person.
forewarned to rub against walls and knock them down onto people. That it became accustomed to rub against walls near people, and they fall on them.
for its own pleasure. For example, to scratch itself, and it did not intend to hurt a person at all.

and the owners are liable for ransom, for it is forewarned etc.. For liability for ransom does not depend on the ox's liability to death, and since it was accustomed to these things, its owner should have guarded it well.
and how is it known that it rubbed for its own pleasure. And not to kill that person.
until their animal kills outside their own property. But if a person entered their property and was killed there, it is not the owners' fault (see above 1:7).
although it is by stoning. As above, halakhah 1, that the ox is liable to stoning wherever it killed.
to claim his wages. For example, a worker of the householder.
or his debt. That he lent him.
stood at the entrance. Of the courtyard.
hin. Yes.
for hin means only stand in your place until I speak with you. That he answered this way to say that he would arrive right away and in the meantime the person should stand where he is.
in the course of its walking. As it walked, without attention and without intent to harm.

for the foot is forewarned to cause damage in the course of its walking. It is the way of an animal to cause damage thus. And since the animal is always forewarned for this, the owner is liable for ransom already the first time it killed in this way, for he should have guarded it well (Maggid Mishneh).

as we have explained. Above 1:7. And only on the injured party's property is one liable for these, but if it trampled a child in the public domain, since one is not liable there for foot damage (ibid. halakhah 10), there is no ransom there either.
the thirty sela fixed in the Torah. Below 11:1.
if it killed unintentionally. In which case it is also exempt from stoning (for if it killed intentionally and became liable to death, one does not pay money for the damage it did - below 11:7).

pays half the value of the slave or the value of the maidservant from its body etc.. For the slave and the maidservant are their owner's property, and since this ox killed them and caused their owner a loss of money, its owner is liable to pay half the damage, as for an innocuous ox that killed its fellow's ox (and see also below 11:4).
how much is the ransom. Given when a forewarned ox kills (above 10:2).

as the judges see etc.. The court estimates the amount of ransom according to the worth of the injured party, viewing him as though he were a slave sold in the market (see Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 1:9).
according to all that is laid upon him. And they learned in the midrash that the verse means an assessment by the court (Mechilta of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai 21:30).
thirty sela. The weight of a sela is 384 average barley grains (Hilchot Shekalim 1:2), and the weight of a grain is 1/20 gram.
fine silver. Clean, without a mixture of copper and the like (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 3:2).
a maneh. A hundred dinars.

and anyone who is held up for a bill of manumission. A slave whose law is to go free but who has not yet been given the bill of release, for example because his master struck him and knocked out his tooth or blinded his eye (see Hilchot Chovel 4:11).
the ransom goes to her heirs from her father. Heirs from her family, namely her sons, and if she has no sons then her heirs from her father (see halakhah le-Moshe mi-Sinai).

and does not go to the husband. Although generally the husband takes precedence in inheriting his wife, this does not apply to property that came to her after her death, which the husband does not inherit, but her children or her father's family do (Hilchot Nachalot 1:11).

one who is half slave and half free. For example, he belonged to two partners and one of them freed him. Although the law is that his master is compelled to free him (Hilchot Avadim 7:7), he is not considered held up for a bill of release, for as long as his master has not actually freed him he is not freed at all (Meiri, Gittin 42b, and commentators on Maimonides, Hilchot Chovel 4:11-12).
he gives half the fine to his master. To his owner, in proportion to his share in the slave.

and the other half should be given etc.. By law, half the fine (fifteen sela) should be given to the owner for his half in which he is a slave, and half the ransom (according to the slave's worth) to the heirs for his half in which he is free. But the law of this slave is that he has no clear heirs (for his betrothal is in doubt - Hilchot Ishut 4:17), and therefore the money remains in the hands of the one who caused the damage (Bavli, Gittin 42b).
and her children came out. She miscarried her fetuses.
exempt from the value of the offspring. And they pay only the woman's damage.
but to a person. A person who in his blow killed the fetus of a woman pays the fetus's value to her husband (Hilchot Chovel 4:1).

for this is like an ox that gored a pregnant donkey. A Canaanite maidservant is her owner's property, and she and her offspring are his. Therefore an ox that gored them is treated as having damaged a pregnant animal, and if it is forewarned its owners are liable for full damages for everything.
and if it was innocuous etc.. He pays half damages from its body, like any innocuous ox that caused damage.
only the ransom fixed in the Torah. And he does not pay for the offspring, since they are considered part of the maidservant's body, and are also included in the ransom payment.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
how do we assess them. The value of the offspring (see also Hilchot Chovel 4:2).
and he gives her owner the loss. The gap between her value as pregnant and her value now.
or half of it. If the ox was innocuous.
and if it killed the maidservant. That in addition to killing the offspring the mother also died, and the killing ox is forewarned.
as we have explained. Above 10:9.
and if it is innocuous etc.. As in all the laws of an ox that causes damage, a person is liable for the damage of his ox even if unintentional.
an innocuous ox that killed and caused damage. And the ox became liable to stoning and its owner to payments.
and we do not judge it under monetary law. The owners are exempt from paying, since an innocuous ox pays its damages only from its body (above 1:7), and it is about to be stoned.
we judge it under monetary law. For the rest of the owners' property is also pledged for payment of the damage.
they came first and judged it under capital law first. The forewarned ox that killed and caused damage, and its sentence of stoning was already finalized.
they again judge it under monetary law. In the manner explained below.
and from where is it paid. For in this case one does not collect from the owners' money, as explained shortly.
from the increase it brought through its plowing. What is earned through the ox's plowing in the field.

after its sentence was finalized. For if from the time its sentence of stoning was finalized until it was actually stoned time passed, the plowing it managed in the meantime is counted as payment due to the injured party (Kesef Mishneh).

it has no owners who would be liable for its damages. From the moment it is to be stoned, it is considered as though it has no owners (see the next halakhah), and if so one cannot obligate its owner to pay for what the ox damaged (see above 8:4). However, although one cannot collect from the owners' property, they assess the ox's damage, and the payment comes from the plowing earnings of the ox (Maggid Mishneh according to Lechem Mishneh's understanding of his words, Yad Peshutah). For although it is as though it has no owners, in practice it is under their authority and profit can be made from its plowing. Moreover, since the judges acted improperly by judging it first to stoning, they caused the injured party to lose, and may therefore collect at least in this way (see Even HaEzel).
we do not judge it under monetary law. For as stated, one does not collect from the owners, and since the ox fled there is no possibility of paying from the earnings of its plowing.
an ox that killed a person. And its sentence was finalized to stoning, as explained in the next paragraph.

and its owners consecrated it, it is not consecrated etc.. For they learned from the verse that an ox whose sentence has been finalized to stoning is forbidden for benefit, and even if it was slaughtered before being stoned, its meat is forbidden for benefit (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:22), and therefore the owners have no ownership in it to consecrate or declare ownerless.
a guardian returned it to its owners. The ox was under the guardian's responsibility when it killed, and after the judgment the guardian returned it.
it is not a return. Because under his hand the ox became worthless, and he must pay the owner of the ox its value.

it is consecrated. So that it is forbidden to benefit from it by the law of sacred property. In any case, the ox is disqualified from being offered, like any animal that killed a person (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:6), and one must wait until a blemish occurs in it, and then redeem it and give its value to the Temple treasury (ibid. halakhah 10). And if after it was consecrated its sentence is finalized to stoning, it is stoned even though it was consecrated (Meiri, Bava Kamma 44b).

and if he declared it ownerless... and if he sold it. In these cases too the ox is stoned if its sentence is finalized to this, except that the one who acquires it from ownerless property or the buyer may meanwhile benefit from the ox, and even slaughter and eat it (ibid.).

this is returned. And the guardian is relieved of returning the deposit. Although the ox will be sentenced to stoning, the guardian is now returning a fit ox, and its owner can do with it as he wishes, for example slaughter and eat it.

as the law of a person. That if he killed they must judge him in his presence, and if he got mixed with others all are exempt from death (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 14:7, Hilchot Rotzeach 4:7). Since the killer is not identified, it is as though he is not before us (Rashi, Sanhedrin 79b).

its sentence was finalized and afterward it got mixed with others, even a thousand. And now all the oxen are forbidden for benefit. For animals are not nullified in a mixture because of their importance (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 16:7), and therefore the forbidden ox that got mixed makes the whole mixture forbidden.
all of them are stoned. In order to fulfill the commandment of stoning an ox that killed (Rashi and other early authorities, Sanhedrin 80a).
and are buried. This is the law of a stoned ox (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashim 19:11).
forbidden for benefit, like any animal that is stoned. For any animal stoned by a court is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:22, Commentary on the Mishnah, Arachin 1:4).
on which a transgression was committed. For example, it was bred by a man and its law is stoning.

its fetus is like it, and its fetus gored, and its fetus was bred. The fetus is considered one of its limbs, as though it shared in the act of transgression and is also subject to the law of stoning (even if it was born before judgment was finalized).

if before its sentence was finalized it became pregnant and gave birth before the judgment was finalized. That between the goring and the finalizing of the sentence it managed to become pregnant and give birth.
its offspring is permitted. Since it was not present at the time of the goring, and at the time of the judgment it was not part of her to receive her sentence.

for the fetus is like the thigh of its mother. It was part of her when the judgment was finalized and became forbidden like her in slaughter and benefit from the meat, but it is not stoned with her because it was not present at the goring (see Yad Ramah, Keter HaMelekh). All this is where she became pregnant before the judgment and gave birth after it, but if she became pregnant and gave birth after the judgment was finalized, her fetus is permitted. For although it was formed in the womb of a forbidden animal, since the father too had a part in forming the offspring, it is not forbidden (Bavli, Sanhedrin 80a, by the law of “this and this cause”; see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:14).
in the prison. The jail.
an ox to be stoned whose witnesses were proven to be conspiring witnesses. Before the stoning the witnesses who testified against the ox were found to be liars, and so the ox is found innocent.

for once its sentence was finalized its owners declared it ownerless. Since once they understood that it is to be stoned, they gave up on it. Therefore even after it became clear that the ox is not to be stoned, it had already left their possession and its law is that of ownerless property that whoever gets to first acquires.
and he refuted the witnesses. He brought conspiring witnesses who proved his innocence.
the ox belongs to its owners. And others cannot acquire it.

for since the owner himself knows that he did not sin... he did not declare it ownerless. Since the owner knows he is innocent, he expects and plans to refute the witnesses and prevent his punishment as well as the stoning of the ox. If so, he never gave up on the ox and did not declare it ownerless.

full of fleeces of wool. Lined with thick pieces of wool. And he is liable even though the cause of death is not the blow from the fall, for liability for a pit is not only when the animal died from the impact (see below, halakhah 14).
and whether an ox or a donkey etc.. But one is not liable under the law of pit for a person who died in it (below, halakhah 16), nor for vessels that were damaged (below 13:1).
but in the usual case. In prevailing reality.
or one who digs on his own property and opened into the public domain. That the pit is diagonal, its bottom on his property and its opening in the public domain.
or opened into his fellow's property. He made the opening in his neighbor's courtyard.
he is liable for its damages. For he is the owner of the pit and responsible for it.

or he declared his pit on his property ownerless or consecrated it, he is exempt. For example, where the public has the right to walk on his property, and nevertheless he is exempt since he declared his pit ownerless (Gra, Choshen Mishpat 410:15). Some explained that the public has no permission there, and indeed the main reason here is not that the pit was declared ownerless but that the injured party had no right to enter (Bach, Sma 410:9, halakhah le-Moshe).
and he dug it originally with permission. But one who digs in the public domain cannot declare it ownerless, and he is responsible for it since he dug it unlawfully (see below 13:5).
that the pit was dug by itself. For example, by a flood.

or an animal or beast dug it. His own or another person's (above 7:6). For example, the pit was dug on his property and then he declared the rest of his property ownerless (as explained above, halakhah 2).
the buyer. Purchaser.

since he is obliged to fill it... he is liable for its damages. Although he does not want this pit at all, it arose on his property and is his possession, and the responsibility to fill it rests on him.
when a man opens. A pit that was covered.
or when a man digs. A new pit.
and if he covered it properly. As detailed below.
even though it was eaten away from within. That woodworms gnawed the pit's cover from the inside, or the cover rotted from within because of the dampness of the pit.
and it cannot withstand camels. Whose great weight may collapse the cover.
and it became weak. It weakened and became fragile.
if camels are not common... he is exempt. For a cover that withstands oxen is enough, and if there are no camels in that place a person need not worry that they will come and ruin the cover.
and if camels come there even occasionally, he is liable. Although they are not always there, since they sometimes come he should have covered it with a more durable cover.
even though camels are common. And he should have covered it with a more durable cover.

since they fell because it was eaten away by worms... he is exempt. Although he was negligent in not covering it properly, and it was ruled above (2:15) that one is liable for an act that began in negligence and ended in accident, that applies only where the negligence caused the accident that could occur. But here there is no connection between his negligence regarding camels and the worms having destroyed it, and therefore he is exempt (see Hilchot Sechirut 3:10 and the rulings and opinions above, 4:1).
one who found a pit, covered it, and then uncovered it again. That it was uncovered and he covered it, and afterward opened it again.

the owner of the pit is liable. For he left the pit uncovered, and should not have relied on the second person's covering. Therefore he is liable even if he saw that the second covered it and did not see that it was uncovered again (Maggid Mishneh).
and this last one is exempt. For he has no share in this pit, and the responsibility does not fall on him for having restored the situation to its previous state.
that he stopped up. Blocked it.

the first one's act was nullified. By filling it with earth the pit was entirely cancelled, and now when the second removed all the earth, it is like digging a new pit and he is at fault for the damages.

a pit of two partners. For example, they had a joint property and dug in it, and then declared their property ownerless without the pit, or there was a pit in the public domain nine handbreadths deep and they completed it together to ten (Bavli, Bava Kamma 51a).

the first is liable until he hands over his bucket to the second etc.. Although both knew that the pit was open and both used it, responsibility rests on the first as long as the bucket is in his hand.
and once he handed his bucket to the second to draw from it etc.. Handing over the bucket shows transfer of responsibility for guarding the pit (see Rabbeinu Chananel and Rashba, Bava Kamma 51b).
and the second came and found it uncovered. For example, the cover was eaten away without the first one's knowledge (Rashi, Bava Kamma 52a).
the second is liable. Because only he saw the pit uncovered, and he is negligent for not covering it.

until the first knows that the pit is uncovered. Until a reasonable time passes in which the first should have visited and checked whether the cover was still there (Yad Peshutah, based on Rabbeinu Yonah Migash cited in Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Kamma 52a, and the Raavad wrote similarly; and see below, halakhah 8, that a pit tends to become uncovered and should therefore be checked). Some explained that he is liable only from the time he actually found out, and until then he is exempt (Maggid Mishneh).
and enough time to hire workers etc.. In addition to the time of knowing that the pit was uncovered, he is also given time to hire workers and obtain materials.
the guardian is liable for its damages. For the responsibility and concern for covering the pit were transferred to him.
even though it was covered. For he handed the pit to them when it was covered.
for a pit is prone to become uncovered. It is the nature of a pit that its cover is destroyed with time, and one must constantly supervise and make sure the cover is proper.

and these have no understanding. For this kind of monitoring of the cover. Therefore one who hands his pit to them is negligent and liable for damages (see above 4:6 for a similar law regarding an ox).
and the owner of the bucket came and took his bucket. Without the pit's owner knowing.
the owner of the pit is liable. For he should not have relied on this cover, and should have anticipated that his fellow would take the bucket.
ditch. A long, narrow excavation.
cave. A wide, square, covered space.
trench. Wide at the bottom and narrow at the top (Rabbeinu Chananel in Shitah Mekubetzet, Bava Kamma 50b).
and why is “pit” stated, if not that it has enough to kill. For an ordinary pit has the depth that is enough to kill one who falls into it.
a depth of ten handbreadths. But less than that, he is exempt for death, as this is classified as an accident (below, halakhah 15).
and if they were injured, the owner of the obstacle is liable for full damages. For damage is common at any height (ibid.).
liable. If the animal died.

for a handbreadth of water counts etc.. A handbreadth full of water adds vapor and heat to the pit like two dry handbreadths, and the vapor of the pit is also one of the causes of death for which the owner of the pit is liable (below, halakhah 14).
if its depth was eight... or its depth was seven etc.. In both these cases, if we count each handbreadth full of water as two handbreadths, we arrive at a pit ten deep.

we do not obligate him to pay. For the matter is in doubt. On the one hand, in these pits there is more water and there may be a lot of vapor, but on the other hand the pit is not deep and the vapor escapes easily (see Maggid Mishneh).
and if the injured party seized, we do not extract from his hand. By the law of seizing in cases of doubt (see above 1:11).
all of them are liable. For all have a share and partnership in the pit.
the first dug less than ten, even a handbreadth. And so the pit is not suitable for killing, only for damaging.
whether he raised a structure on its edge a handbreadth. And so now there are ten handbreadths from the floor of the pit to the top of the addition that was built.

this last one is liable. Both for death of those who die in the pit and for damage of those injured in it. And although the first too has a share in the pit (at least regarding damages), since the second completed it to ten he created a new type of pit suitable also for killing, and it is as though the first one's acts were cancelled (Tosafot and Rashba, Bava Kamma 51a).
he filled in the handbreadth he added. Filled in the depth of the excavation he added.
or demolished the handbreadth he built. On the edge of the pit.

it is in doubt whether the first one's act has already been cancelled. From the moment the second created a pit of ten handbreadths, the pit is considered in his domain, and now he is responsible for future damages and the first is exempt.
or not yet cancelled. And since the second undid his acts, the first returns to being responsible for the damages.
and an ox fell into it. From the side of the pit that existed before the second one widened it.
if it died from its vapor. From the heat and density of the air.
for he reduced its vapor. For widening the pit actually thinned the vapor, and so the second is not responsible at all for the ox's death.
and if it died from the impact. From striking the walls and floor of the pit.

for he brought closer the damage of this pit. Although the ox fell on the side the first dug and which was not widened, the second increased the danger to one who falls by adding surface area to the walls and floor, and a faller may roll and be struck more (Yad Peshutah; and see Lechem Mishneh and Perisha, Choshen Mishpat 410, who explained in other ways).
and likewise if the ox fell from the side that the last one widened. And died either from impact or from vapor.
for he brought closer the damage of this pit. Although widening the pit reduced the vapor, it is what caused the animal to fall, since it fell in the place that was widened.
and if it fell from the side that the first dug. And died from the vapor.
the first is liable, for this last one reduced its vapor. But if it died from the impact, the last is liable, as explained in the previous paragraph.
from its vapor. The air and heat of the pit, for example it suffocated.
from its impact. The striking of the body on the ground.
the depth of the pit equals its width. That the measure of the pit's depth equals the measure of its width.
it has no vapor. For such a pit is quite ventilated.
and if it was not struck. If it is known that it was not injured in its limbs by the blow of the fall, for example the whole pit was lined (above halakhah 1).
exempt. For at such a depth the vapor in it does not ordinarily kill. And the fact that the animal that fell there died is exceptional.
and the animal was struck in it. Fell from it and hit the ground.
he is liable to pay. For liability for the impact of falling into a pit includes every case of falling from a height.
for damage at any height is common and known. For even a small obstacle commonly causes damage to an animal, and therefore he is liable for damage at any height.
and it is like an accident. If the animal died from a low height, and therefore he is exempt for that.
a young one. That has not yet been taught to plow, and does not yet know to protect itself from pits (Meiri, Bava Kamma 53b).
blind. Sightless.
or that fell at night. In all these the animal could not protect itself from falling.
sighted. Of sound sense.
for this is like an accident. And it is not common.
because it is the way of an animal to see and turn away from obstacles. Therefore the blame should not be placed on the owner of the pit.
and likewise if a person fell into it and died... he is exempt. For they learned from the verse that one is exempt for the death of a person in a pit (below 13:1).
and if the person was injured. For the verse excluded only the death of a person and not a case where he was injured (see Rashi, Bava Kamma 28a).
or the sighted animal. For a sighted animal avoids obstacles that might kill it but does not necessarily notice hazards that might injure it (Maggid Mishneh).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1, that one is liable for full damages for a pit.
an ox of disqualified consecrated animals fell into it. An ox designated for an offering that was disqualified (for example, a blemish occurred in it), whose law is to be redeemed.

as it is stated, “and the dead animal shall be his”. At the beginning of the verse it says “the owner of the pit shall pay, he shall return money to its owner”, and it is learned that only when the carcass of the ox belongs to the injured party (“and the dead animal shall be his”) is the owner of the pit obliged to pay.

this one is excluded, for it is forbidden for benefit and its law is to be buried. Even if it was already redeemed (in which case one is liable for its goring, as above 8:1), it is permitted for benefit only after slaughter, when it may be eaten (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:9), and now that it died its law is to be buried.
and the animal fell into the pit from the sound of the digging. It was frightened by the noise and fell into it.
and turned back on its heel. Backward, into the pit behind it.
outside the pit. It fell on the ground in front of it.
the court does not obligate him. The owner of the pit, since the ox was not injured in the pit itself.
we do not extract from his hand. For in any case the digging of the pit caused the damage, and there is doubt here.
the owner of the pit is exempt. Just as he is exempt where the ox fell backward into the pit.
an ox that pushed an animal into the pit. If so, the owner of the ox and the owner of the pit are partners in the damage.

and if it is innocuous, the owner of the ox pays a quarter from its body. Since the law of an innocuous ox is to pay half of what it damaged, the owner of the ox pays only half of his half, that is a quarter, and the payment is from the body of the ox that caused the damage, as in all payments of an innocuous ox.
and the owner of the pit pays three parts. For he must make up the damage the owner of the ox does not pay.
the loss in value of the carcass. The difference between the ox's value when alive and its value now.
I have a claim against you. That my dead ox is in your pit and you are responsible for it.
even though it is large and sighted. And it was explained above (halakhah 16) that in such a case he is exempt.
since it was pushed, it is like one that fell at night. It could not avoid falling, and if so you bear the responsibility.
whatever I can extract from the owner of the ox, I extract. For certainly the owner of the ox too is a partner in the damage.
and the rest you are liable to pay. You are obliged to complete the damage because of your responsibility.
one who places the stone pays half etc.. Because they are partners in the death of the ox.

and an ox of disqualified consecrated animals. Designated for an offering and disqualified. It was already explained above (8:1) that disqualified consecrated animals that were redeemed are liable for damages, but here it speaks of those that were not redeemed, and therefore they are not classed as “his fellow's ox” and are exempt (Maggid Mishneh).
if it is innocuous. And it would be proper for him to pay half of his half, which is a quarter.

the one belonging to the ordinary person pays half damages. Since an ox of disqualified consecrated animals is not liable for payments, it is viewed as if the ordinary person's ox gored alone, and he pays half damages like an ordinary innocuous ox.
and the rest from you. For both oxen gored together and in effect each is fully responsible for the damage, and therefore when needed the owner of the ordinary ox will pay more.
the owner of the ox is exempt. From paying ransom, for the blame is on the one who dug, who placed an obstacle there. And since it was not intentional, the ox too is not stoned (above 10:9).
the owner of the ox takes the value of his ox etc.. For the owner of the pit was responsible for the damages of the ox that fell into it.
from the heirs of the owners. In the manner explained above 8:11-12.
from tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.

“an ox”, not a person; “a donkey”, not vessels. The exemption for a person applies only when he died and not when he was injured (above 12:16), but for vessels he is exempt even if they were damaged and not entirely broken. For vessels have no death status and their damage is their death (Rashi, Bava Kamma 28b).
even if an ox fell with its vessels. Fell with vessels on it, which is more likely to happen.
and its derivatives are like it, forewarned from the start. For they contain an obstacle and are likely to cause damage (and see above 2:1).
whether he declared the obstacle ownerless. In any case he is responsible for the obstacle as though he had not declared it ownerless (see below, halakhah 5).
or his straw and chaff. See below, halakhah 14.
in the public domain. Or in a place from which they are likely to fall into the public domain, such as on his roof (halakhah le-Moshe, Yad Peshutah).
and likewise if he placed them on his property... and did not declare them ownerless. As explained regarding one who digs a pit (above 12:2).
stumbled on the ground and was thrown onto this obstacle and was hurt by it. That as a result of stumbling on the ground he slipped and fell onto the obstacle and was injured by it.
the owner of the obstacle is liable. Although the start of the damage was caused by the ground, since in the end he was injured by the obstacle, the owner of the obstacle is liable.
or were soiled. For example, he spilled water in the public domain and this person's vessels were soiled by it (below, halakhah 12).
for it is not the way of people to look carefully etc.. And the owner of the jug should have known that people might stumble on his jug.
for he has no right to place them in the first place. For example here, where one may not leave vessels in the public domain except for a short time, to rest (see above 3:3).
the place of the winepress corners. The area near the grape press where people place their jars when the press is full (Meiri, Bava Kamma 28a).
because he should have looked. For it is known that people place their jars in this place.

he is exempt for its breakage etc.. For he could not have protected himself from stumbling on the jar, and if so the owner of the jar is the one who should have refrained from placing his jars in this state.
his jar broke in the public domain. By mistake, for example he stumbled on something.
was hurt by its shards. Was injured by the broken pieces.
exempt by human law. And one cannot obligate him to pay for the damage.
because he is coerced. It was not through his fault that he stumbled and the vessel broke.
and liable by the laws of Heaven. Although a court cannot obligate him, morally he is responsible for what happened and ought to pay.
and the shards and water are like ownerless property etc.. This is the reason for the exemption, for presumably a person does not want the shards.

and he declared them ownerless only after he was coerced. Therefore, although declaring an obstacle ownerless does not ordinarily exempt (above, halakhah 2), here he is exempt since the damage began by accident.
and the same law applies if his camel fell. And he abandoned it.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.
potters. Sellers of earthenware.
if the first could have stood up. That he could have stood up before the damage occurred.

and he can stand up. Unlike shards of clay or water (above, halakhah 7), a person's body is not ownerless, and even if he fell by accident he is responsible to stand up and prevent damage (Rif, Bava Kamma 14b).
exempt. Because he is still coerced.
because he is preoccupied with himself. By the fall.
and every obstacle is a derivative of pit. And this person too, since he is lying in the road, is like other obstacles lying around that are classed as derivatives of pit.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 2.
and glassmakers. Sellers of glass vessels.
and each of them could have stood up and did not. And they are at fault for the damage caused by their bodies.
whether he was injured by the body of the first. For the body of the first is like a pit, since he should have stood up (above, halakhah 8).

or was injured by his load. In this case it can be assumed that he did not abandon his load that fell (for a glassmaker does not abandon his merchandise), and therefore it is considered his pit (Ramban, Milchamot Hashem, Bava Kamma 15a in the pages of the Rif; and see Maggid Mishneh).
but if he was injured by the second's load... he is exempt. Even if the second did not abandon the load that caused the damage.

for the first caused the second to fall with his load. And he is responsible for the second's load becoming an obstacle to the public. Nevertheless the first too is exempt for the damage, since this load is not his property and he is treated like one who abandons his load after being coerced, who is exempt. And for what the second caused to the third by his body he is liable, for he should have stood up and did not (Ramban there).
and if they warned one another. That each warned his fellow not to collide with him.
exempt. Even if they could have stood up.
and another was injured by them. Bodily harm.
he is liable for its damages. For the law of this water is like a pit.
and if his vessels were soiled. His clothes were dirtied by the water.
exempt. Like all derivatives of pit, for which he is exempt regarding vessels.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 3.
the water was absorbed into the ground... he is liable for its damages. For the water caused him to slip and be struck on the ground.
who open their drains. Open the sewage pipes of the house to the public domain.
and clean out their cisterns. Empty the water reservoirs of the water gathered in them so that new rainwater can enter.
but in the rainy season they have permission to pour. Since rain falls anyway.
they are liable for full damages. Under the laws of pit damages, and although they did so with permission, responsibility for the damage rests on them (and see below, halakhah 15).
his straw. The remains of the stalks left on the threshing floor after threshing.
and his chaff. The part of the stalk that remains in the ground after harvest (Meiri, Bava Kamma 30a).

that they may thresh them. That people will tread on them so that they are crushed and improve the ground as fertilizer. The reason for the prohibition is that people are liable to slip on straw and chaff (Bavli, Bava Kamma 30b).

the Sages fined him... from the time they were trodden and improved. From the time they improved, they announce that these are ownerless, so that the one who put them out in violation will not profit.

and if someone came first and acquired them from the time of removal... we do not extract from his hand. For in practice the one who put them out is already fined from the time he put out the straw and chaff, and therefore if someone took them they are his. But we do not instruct so initially, and if a person asks in advance we tell him not to take them (Yad Peshutah; and see Maggid Mishneh, who explained that the reason is that there is doubt whether one can acquire them already from the time of removal, and therefore if he seized, we do not extract from his hand).
and although they are like ownerless property etc.. For the declaration of ownerlessness was meant to fine him, but responsibility for damage remains on him as long as others have not acquired them.
every person may. It is permitted.
take out the manure and the droppings. That accumulate in his courtyard.
manure. Agricultural waste used for fertilizing.
at the time of taking out manure. A time when people customarily take out and place manure in the public domain to improve it.
be trampled. Trodden, and thereby softened.
and nevertheless. That it was permitted.
and they are liable for this dung as theft. For it was not declared ownerless, and there is even permission to place it.

since it gains nothing from being trampled etc.. For this reason it is forbidden to take the dung except at the time of taking out manure. And although at this time it is forbidden to place it in the public domain, since it does not improve through treading they did not need to enact a rule and fine the owner for it, and therefore taking it is theft (see Hilchot Gezelah 6:5).
one does not soak clay. In water to make it soft.
in the public domain. Since soaking takes a long time and in the meantime this is an obstacle.
and one does not bake bricks. Dry them in the public domain.
but one may knead clay. Mix it with water to put it right away into the building.
but not for bricks. One does not knead clay to prepare bricks, for this clay requires longer standing (Tiferet Yisrael, Bava Metzia 10:7).
one who builds in the public domain. Who builds on his property and needs the space of the public domain to bring building materials there (Meiri, Bava Metzia 118b).
the one who brings stones brings etc.. He should not leave the stones lying, but as soon as they are put down there the builder takes them.
and all of them who caused damage... full damages. Although they acted as permitted, as said above, halakhah 15.
the quarryman. A quarrier of stone for building.
and handed it to the stonecutter. The one who levels and smooths the stone.
the stonecutter is liable. For while the stone was in his possession he had to see that people would not trip on it.
to the donkey driver. The one who carries the stone on a donkey to the building site.
to the porter. A carrier who hands it to the builder.
to the builder. The one who stands next to the building wall.
to the one who sets its seat in the building. Who is responsible for the stone sitting exactly and firmly.
a course. A row of stones in a building.
fell and caused damage. And it was not in anyone's hands.
and they were working by contract. That they received a sum in advance for the whole job.
all of them are liable. For responsibility for the work rests on them together.
and by hire. That each received wages for his time of work.
the last is liable. For he is responsible for the stone sitting steadily and not causing damage.
the wall and the tree. Of an individual.
and caused damage. After they fell, people were hurt by them (Even HaEzel; and the Maggid Mishneh explained that they caused damage as they fell).
exempt. Their owners, even if he knew that they fell.

and even though he declared them ownerless. The commentators found these words difficult, since apparently if he declared them ownerless there is more reason to be lenient (see Sma and Be'er HaGolah). One explanation is that the owner is exempt even though he had the ability to remove them and did not do so but left them lying and declared them ownerless. The reason he is exempt is that they are not like a pit, since from the start they are not an obstacle at all, and he was therefore coerced when they fell. And since the obstacle arose through accident, its owner may declare it ownerless and be exempt, as explained above, halakhah 7 (Even HaEzel).
they fell within the time... exempt. Although he knew and did not remove them, as stated at the beginning of the halakhah.

liable. For after the set time they are presumed dangerous and likely to cause damage, and if they fell, declaring them ownerless will not help, since they are like any pit that began in negligence (see above, halakhah 2).
one who hides the thorn and the glass. In his wall.
and they protruded into the public domain. That these projected into the public domain.
is liable for full damages. For he left an obstacle for the public.
within his property. And they did not project outward.
if it was a weak wall. And about to collapse.
the one who hid them is liable. For he should have assumed that the wall would fall (or be demolished by its owner), and the thorns and glass would be exposed.
the owner of the wall is liable. For he should have guarded against creating this obstacle and removed the thorns and glass after demolishing the wall.
so that the plow will not bring them up. And they would be exposed and could cause damage. But to a depth of three handbreadths the plow does not reach.
he may not clear stones. Remove stones.
and not pits, ditches, or caves. Different kinds of excavations.
and although a wagon can travel over them etc.. Because he made a strong cover for them.

lest it open from below. Because of time and people passing there (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 3:11). Although it is forbidden to dig in the public domain, if he did so and covered it properly he is exempt (above 12:4).
and one who digs a pit for the needs of the public. So that they may drink and benefit from its water.
and like balconies. Porches, a kind of veranda.
above a camel and its rider. For above this height it is not reasonable that a person would pass.
provided that he does not darken the road for those in the public domain. Even when it was permitted to build them at a great height, it is on condition that they not shade and darken the road.
and if he wished. To build them lower.
he draws in to his own. He demolishes the house wall and rebuilds it slightly inward.
and extends out. The projections, so that they do not project into the public domain.
but he cannot return walls to their place. And thereby prevent people from walking there again.

for any boundary that people have taken hold of etc.. Although it was his domain, once he vacated this area and the public walked on it, it may not be returned to private domain (see below, halakhah 27).
boundary. Border, road.
projections. Protrusions sticking out from the wall.

they remain in their presumption. We assume that the one who put out the projections did so within his own area and lawfully, and later the area underneath became public domain (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Batra 3:11).
that leans toward the public domain. And its branches extend into it.

and they leave an empty space from the two banks of the river etc.. For sometimes it is necessary to tow the boat with ropes and it is more convenient to do so on the bank of the river and not in it. Trees standing there must be cut down to clear space for those towing boats, so that they will not be harmed.
the width of the sailors' shoulders. A measure in which they can tow comfortably, and some wrote that it is about two cubits (Meiri, Bava Metzia 107b, but see Hilchot Genevah 8:2).
he took it. Kept it for himself.
and gave them from the side. An alternative path at the side of his field.
what he gave he gave. For the public already acquired it and held it.

and how wide is the public road etc.. The definition of a public road for many matters (Sabbath domains, sale of land and more) is a road sixteen cubits wide (and see Pitchei Teshuvah and Arukh HaShulchan, that for the matter mentioned here even a small path that the public has taken hold of may not be removed from the public's possession).
and the fire passed. And caused damage in its burning.
the one who kindled the fire shall surely pay. And even if he did not actually kindle but was negligent in guarding it (below, halakhah 4).
and burning is among the primary categories of damage. Among the main types of damage, and its derivatives are like it (below, halakhah 16).
from the end of the boundary. From the end of the border between his property and his fellow's.
everything according to the height of the flame. For a large fire needs more distance so that it will not cause damage.
it is a plague from Heaven. And it could not have been foreseen at all.
a channel. A water conduit from which small ditches are drawn to irrigate other places through them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Peah 2:1).
exempt. For generally this measure is enough to stop the fire from spreading.
we estimate the height of the fence etc.. For all of these together determine whether the fire could pass in the normal situation.
a boring fire. That stays in place and bores through and burns (Arukh, entry “kadach”).
a great flame that rises and bends from the height of the flame's ascent. That the flame is tall and bends and spreads to the sides.
and there was wood there. So that the fire could spread over long distances.
and a fence fell. That separates his property from another's.
not because of the fire. But if it fell because of the fire he is liable in any case, since he did not keep the fire properly distant.

to his ox that went out and caused damage etc.. It is like one who leaves his ox in a pen and did not lock properly (above 4:1), and here too he should have fenced and prevented the fire from causing damage.
one who sends the fire. Brought them something that caused a fire.
exempt by human law. For he did not cause the damage, and it was not reasonable that a fire would develop from this.
and liable by the laws of Heaven. Although a court cannot obligate him, morally he is responsible for what happened and ought to pay.
a coal. Without an actual flame.

for it is the way of a coal to go out on its own. And therefore he is exempt by human law, since the fire was caused only because of their fanning, and they too are exempt since they lack understanding.
a flame. Open fire, which tends to spread unless properly guarded.
for his acts caused it. And he should not have entrusted the flame to those who are not capable of guarding.
he sent the fire with a sensible person. Even if it was an actual flame.
this sensible person who kindled it is liable. For by taking the fire he took responsibility for it, and he is at fault for its damages.
the fire. The flame.
and one brought the wood. Afterward, so that the fire could keep burning.
the one who brought the wood is liable. For without him the fire would not have continued.
the one who brought the fire is liable. Here too the last is liable, for without him the wood does not cause damage at all.
another came and fanned it. For after the acts of the first ones the fire would not have flared up on its own, and this one came and fanned it.
a wind that is not common. That does not blow constantly even though it comes many times, and all the more a storm wind that blows only rarely (Maggid Mishneh).
all of them are exempt. If by their acts they did not cause the fire to flare up, for they could not have known that such a wind would come afterward and kindle the fire.
he fanned it and the wind fanned it. That his fanning and the wind's together caused the fire to ignite.
for he caused. This fire together with the wind.
he pays full damages etc.. Like anyone whose property caused damage, who pays full damages and from the best of his property (above 1:7).
stones. It damaged them by its burning.
or earth. For example, it struck plowed ground (Bavli, Bava Kamma 60a).
or the field. Even things that fire does not ordinarily consume, such as the ground and stones.
threshing sledges. A morag is a grooved wooden board or one with protrusions used for threshing.
they were clothes, glass vessels, and the like. That people do not usually hide in a stack.

exempt for the vessels. Nevertheless he must pay for the place of the vessels as though it had been full of grain, as explained in the next halakhah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 6:7, Maggid Mishneh).
exempt for all the vessels hidden in the stack. Even for those that are customarily hidden.
but he pays the measure of the place of the vessels etc.. We view the place of the vessels as full of grain, and he pays for this quantity of grain.
as though it were full of a stack of wheat or barley. According to what is in the stack.
and a kid was tied to it. To the stack.
liable. For the kid, and exempt for the slave since he could have fled (Maggid Mishneh).
for it is the way of people to do so with a stack. A person tends to tie his kids to the stack, and therefore the one who set the fire is liable for it.

if a slave was bound... exempt. For the kid, and liable for the death of the slave, since he is liable to death for the slave, and the rule is that one who does an act that carries liability to death is exempt from paying for other things (see Hilchot Genevah 3:1).
one who lends a place to his fellow. On his property so that he may place his stack there.
and the lender kindled etc.. Lit a fire on his property and it burned the stack.
pays only the value of the stack alone. For he did not lend it on the understanding that he would hide things there.
he lent him a place to stack wheat etc.. In all these he pays only the value of barley, which is cheaper than wheat.
to stack wheat and he stacked barley. He pays only the value of barley, for that is what he damaged.
to stack barley and he stacked wheat. He gave permission only for barley, and therefore he will not pay more than its value.
or he stacked wheat and covered it with barley. He pays the value of barley, for the wheat is considered hidden inside the barley (Tosafot of Rabbeinu Peretz, Bava Kamma 62a).
or he stacked barley and covered it with wheat. For he gave permission only for barley.
the dwelling. A large building.
for it is the way of people etc.. As stated above (halakhah 8), one who kindles on his fellow's property is liable for hidden vessels that it is the way of people to put there.
and whatever the householder claims. That was in the house and burned.
swears while holding a sacred object. Holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
and takes. Payment for the damage.
as will be explained. Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 1:2.

things he is estimated to have etc.. Items that can be estimated to be in his possession, or that were deposited with him for safekeeping (and so is the law for anyone who damaged his fellow's property and does not know what he damaged; see Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:17-19).
because he overloaded. That he loaded his camel with a load that extended into private domains.
whether the animal stood. And during that time the fire spread.
or did not stand. But as it walked the flax entered and kindled the dwelling.
